Kiley McDaniel covers MLB prospects, the MLB Draft and more, including trades and free agency.
Co-author of Author of 'Future Value'Follow on X
TheMLB offseasonhas officially started! As free agency begins, it's time for our annual ranking of the top 50 free agents in the class and predicting how much money each player will get.
The story of this market is threefold:Tarik Skubalis the clear top free agent, with a strong chance to break some pitcher contract records. Meanwhile, the rest of the market is weaker than usual, and the Dec. 1 end of the current CBA deal looms. Before the last CBA expired, there was a flurry of activity or largely above-expectations deals. So do teams mirror that behavior? And does the lesser talent base affect that? I have my projected spending (about $2.65 billion in guarantees) down about 12.5% from last winter's actual spending (a little over $3 billion) due to less high-end talent.
Here is a quick look at what else you need to know for these rankings and projections.
Free agents are ranked by the size of their projected guaranteed contracts plus the posting fee, not the quality of the player. I explain in the blurb when I'm projecting a contract that's not the biggest guarantee they will be offered, normally if the player had a down season and wants to hit the market next winter on better terms. The contract projections are a mix of my opinions and those of agents and executives, but the goal is to predict what will happen, not decide what each player is worth.
The four projected candidates from Japan's NPB and South Korea's KBO have already been posted as their 45-day window will be open past the extremely likely Dec. 1 lockout, so there isn't any guessing about when or if they will be posted as there normally is at this juncture of the offseason.
One other term to know is the qualifying offer (QO): Teams can offer an eligible free agent a one-year, $23.15 million deal, and if they turn it down and sign with another team, the original team gets compensation. If a player gets a QO and turns it down, it normally negatively affects their market, so I've noted it for players below.
For the players who landed big league deals last winter, I projected 9% more in guarantees than they got, but that was driven more by those players signing for 6% fewer guaranteed years than I projected, with a number of higher-end free agents doing a version of whatKyle TuckerandBo Bichetteultimately did, taking AAV instead of years.
Projected contract/QO:eight years, $352 million (44 AAV), not eligible for QO
As the playoffs began, Ipolled27 industry insiders about Skubal's contract and got an average projection of eight years, $355 million (44.6 AAV), with 59% of projections landing just above the all-time pitcher guaranteed money record of $325 million (byYoshinobu Yamamoto, over 12 years) and the big, round number of $400 million. The all-time pitcher-only AAV record is $43.3 million, set byMax Scherzer, is the other mark to beat. Seventy-eight percent of the panel thought Skubal would sign before the very likely Dec. 1 lockout.
That means the smart money is a pretty quick process that ends with a contract guarantee between $300 million and $400 million and beats the Scherzer AAV mark. Over the years, I've also found that the total guarantee for the top player on the market tends to beat the average of these panel projections and is usually a notch higher than I think they will be, and that is how I landed at just short of $400 million; a bit over wouldn't surprise me.
My read on the market from further talks with industry people is that it's about a two-thirds chance the guarantee will land in the $325-400 million area, and a slightly higher chance it's a high-AAV shorter deal (such as three years, $150 million with two opt-outs) than over $400 million; call it 68%, 20%, and 12%, respectively.
I ended up a bit below the panel average as a slight hedge toward the lower guarantee outcome. Kyle Tucker and Bo Bichette from last winter's class don't have that much in common with Skubal, and people think Skubal will go for the biggest guarantee, but it's hard to ignore that teams seem more interested than ever in these shorter deals with elite talents.
Skubal won't win a third consecutive American League Cy Young this year, both because he was traded between leagues and because of a midseason elbow procedure that affected his innings total this year. He was basically as good on a per-inning basis this year as the past two seasons, but he missed five starts in 2026. On the flip side, some teams are wary of offering a record-breaking deal to Skubal because of his history of arm issues: Tommy John surgery in 2016 while in college, a 2022 surgery on the flexor tendon in his throwing elbow and a 2026 procedure toremovea loose elbow particle. Add in that he's turning 30 years old in November and a number of teams just won't offer a retail price on a long deal to any pitcher with those risk factors.
As covered in that panel piece, the usual suspects are believed to be at the front of the line for Skubal: The Dodgers and Mets are the primary bidders, the Tigers are monitoring for a discount, the Yankees are thinking about it (and then trading from their pitching stockpile if they land Skubal), and the Angels, White Sox, and Padres are the sleepers with ownership changes behind the interest.

Padres predicted to poach Dodgers' $32M two-time Cy Young winner in 'motivated' free agency move | Sporting NewsSkip to main content
Padres predicted to poach Dodgers' $32M two-time Cy Young winner in 'motivated' free agency move
TheLos Angeles Dodgershave a lot of questions surrounding their offseason as a potential new agreement with the MLB could make them watch their payroll. If that is the case, all eyes are going to be on Tarik Skubal.
The two-time Cy Young winner is a free agent for the first time in his career.The good news for the Dodgers is that Skubal enjoyed his time in LA.
“The sense I get from people that he has talked to, is that he would love to be a Los Angeles Dodger. He loved his time in LA. I think it's a perfect marriage in LA," MLB insider Jim Bowden said.
However, other teams are not going to go down without a fight in their pursuit of Skubal. The division-rivalSan Diego Padresare expected to be searching for starting pitching, especially following Michael King's latest free-agency decision.
“Right-handed starter Michael King has declined the player option on his contract with the Padres to become a free agent, sources told MLB.com on Thursday. The club has not confirmed the news on King, who will now become one of the top arms on the market entering his age-32 season,"MLB.com's AJ Cassavell wrote.
For this reason, CBS Sports' Mike Axisa believes the Padres could poach Skubal from the Dodgers.
“I'll go off the board a bit and say the Padres. The new ownership group didn't pay $3.9 billion for the franchise only to cheap out in their first offseason. They're moneyed and motivated, and that's usually enough to land the top free agents. It should appeal to Skubal too. The Padres are in the postseason most years, they play in a great (and largely pitcher-friendly) ballpark, and it's San Diego. How can you not love San Diego? Skubal to the Padres because the new owners want to make a big splash in their first offseason. That's my prediction,”Axisa wrote.
Landing Skubal would be one of the biggest wins of the offseason for any team, and it would be even sweeter for San Diego knowing it took him away from its hated division rival. Skubal would then become the ace of another California team with an exciting brand of baseball.
Skubal played on a $32 million contract last season that was split between the Detroit Tigers and Dodgers.San Diego is expected to be aggressive, but the biggest question is whether it will be enough to pry him away from LA.

Multiple AuthorsNov 4, 2026, 07:00 AM ET
Just two weeks into the NBA season, storylines have been flipped as injuries and surprise surges reverberate around the league.
ThePhiladelphia 76ershave dominated their opponents early -- and arehaving some funin the process. Meanwhile, the reigning championNew York Knicksare attempting toclaw themselvesback into the top echelon after starting the season 0-3.
It's in the West where things have started to heat up. TheOklahoma City ThunderandMinnesota Timberwolvesare dealing with injuries to their stars, making way for players such as theMemphis Grizzlies'Ty Jerometo have an early impact in his team's standings. TheLos Angeles Lakers'Luka Doncicis making an early MVP case and doesn't seem to be slowing down after scoring 42 and 45 points in his past two games. And thePortland Trail Blazers, sansJa Morantas hedeals with an injury, are showing that depth is what will set teams apart across the league.
In our second iteration of Power Rankings since the season started, our NBA insiders assigned four words to describe each team's start to 2026-27, and break down why things are -- or are not -- working.
Note: Team rankings are based on where members of our panel (ESPN's Jamal Collier, Michael C. Wright, Tim MacMahon, Dave McMenamin, Vincent Goodwill, Zach Kram, Ben Golliver, Kris Rhim and Anthony Slater) think teams belong.
Next games:vs. MIN (Nov. 4), @ PHX (Nov. 7), vs. DEN (Nov. 9)
VanVleet's impact is immeasurable. The Rockets navigated the choppy waters ofKevin Durant's first season nearly rudderless without floor generalFred VanVleet, who sustained a season-ending knee injury before the start of training camp. Nowthat he's back, Houston is a calmer, more organized team. VanVleet directs traffic, manipulates defenses to set up teammates for shots in their preferred spots and limits turnovers, catalyzing a Houston offense with the league's best rating (121.2).
Wisely, the Rockets added ballhandling insurance with another veteran point guard inMarcus Smart, who can start in VanVleet's place when he sits the second night of back-to-backs.-- Michael C. Wright
Next games:vs. PHI (Nov. 4), vs. LAL (Nov. 8), vs. WAS (Nov. 9)
3-pointers have improved.The Pistons have developed a reputation for stifling defense and it hasn't changed, being first in points per game against and defensive rating. What has seemed to improve early is their 3-point shooting.
Cade Cunninghamis carrying over his playoff 3-point shooting with a career-high 37%, andKevin Huerter, who struggled after coming from Chicago at midseason, is at a more-than-respectable clip of 38.5% (he shot 29% in 25 games last season).Duncan Robinsonis No. 4 in makes, and the team collectively has risen to No. 6 in percentage (38.1). Their season high in triples in a game in 2025-26 was 18, a mark they've matched twice in the first two weeks.-- Vince Goodwill
Next games:@ DET (Nov. 4), @ CLE (Nov. 6), @ CHI (Nov. 8), vs. BOS (Nov. 10)
The Tyrese Maxey Show.Maxey has been Philly's best player while being on a team with two former MVPs,LeBron JamesandJoel Embiid, and a Finals MVP inJaylen Brown. The 25-year-old leads the Sixers in scoring and has buoyed them late in games this season with explosive fourth quarters that have kept them winning. He leads the NBA in fourth-quarter scoring (11.0).
"I just think he now feels -- like in a nonarrogant and even a humble way -- he knows he's really, really good," coach Nick Nurse said of Maxey. "And I'm not sure that was always the case."-- Kris Rhim
Next games:vs. MIL (Nov. 4), @ CHA (Nov. 6), @ MIL (Nov. 8), @ PHI (Nov. 10)
They'll be just fine.The CelticstradedAll-NBA forward Brown fresh off his best season for 36-year-oldPaul Georgethis offseason, a return that came as somewhat of a surprise considering George appears to be declining.
But through the first two weeks, George has fit in with the Celtics seamlessly as the team has looked like a contender in the Eastern Conference. George is averaging 20.7 points, six rebounds and five assists. Coach Joe Mazzulla recently praised George's impact for being "beyond what's happening on the offensive end," pointing to George's leadership.-- Rhim
Next games:vs. DAL (Nov. 4), @ SAC (Nov. 6), @ POR (Nov. 7), @ PHX (Nov. 9)
Still working through kinks.San Antonio expected that, coming into the season, it would have to work through some hiccups with its new starting lineup, but Spurs coach Mitch Johnson is committed to seeing it through. Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition (2026) review: Updated in all the right places
Are you willing to pay $50 more for the upgrades?
ByBilly SteeleOct. 28, 2026 9:00 am ESTBilly Steele for EngadgetAdd Engadget on Google:Preferred SourceGoogle DiscoverRATING :8.6 / 10Pros
High-contrast display with crisp text
Aluminum back cover a color-matched front are both upgrades
More expensive than the previous model was at launch
Wireless charging ditched for new accessories
Signature Edition features don’t feel like must-haves
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
There's no denying the chokehold Amazon has on the ereader industry. Its library is massive and its entire lineup of Kindles are consistently reliable devices that meet readers with varying budgets and needs. As part ofthe company's 2026 lineup, theKindle Paperwhite Signature Edition ($250)sits squarely in the middle in terms of both capabilities and price. Amazon saw fit to refine an already compelling mix of design and performance, with key changes to how you use this Paperwhite as well. But as we noted with the2024 Signature Edition, the best premium ereader may not offer any exclusive features that you can't live without.
Amazon didn't try to reinvent the wheel with its updates to the more premium Paperwhite. There's now an aluminum back, but overall, it's still an IPX8 waterproof design with a high-contrast, 300 dpi display (more on the screen changes later) and 32GB of storage. The company did color match the front bezels on the Seaglass Green version so it matches the back panel. This is certainly a welcome change as it definitely looks better than previous models that had colorful cases but with gray fronts. The 2026 model is also one millimeter thinner than its predecessor — a variation you're unlikely to notice, but one Amazon will gladly tout.
Amazon also moved the power button to the top right edge, a location that will be more familiar for anyone who uses a smartphone. I honestly prefer it there, because even though I've been using a regular Kindle Paperwhite since 2024, I never got used to the power button on the bottom edge. Now, the USB-C port is the only component that still resides there.
Perhaps the biggest change on the 2026 Paperwhite Signature Edition is the introduction of pogo pins on the back cover. Amazon ditched the 2024 model's standard wireless charging (via Qi-compatible and Amazon accessories) in favor of this arrangement. The four pins accommodate new accessories, most notably thePage Turn Cover ($80)with physical page-turn buttons, and there's alsoa $60 charging standwith an unknown shipping date. I should note that both of these accessories also work with the Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition, which has the requisite pogo pins onboard as well.
In my opinion, the Paperwhite line offers the best reading experience on a Kindle. I don't need a color screen, but I do prefer the adjustable warm light and larger display over the standard Kindle. Of course, the IPX8 waterproofing is also nice to have, as I like to take the Paperwhite to the beach, and you can certainly feel safe using it during a bath or at the pool.
To further enhance the overall experience, Amazon employs an oxide-thin film transistor backplane and offers a contrast ratio that it says is its highest yet. The company promises deeper blacks and crisper text on the 2026 Signature Edition compared to the previous version, although my eyes are unable to discern the difference in either of those. I couldn't distinguish between the sharpness on my 2024 Paperwhite and this new Signature model either, but I could tell them apart by the slightly warmer overall glow of the latest release, even when the Warmth slider on both Paperwhites was set to 0. Still, the Paperwhite display continues to offer the best ereader performance among the company's lineup for my money.
The auto-adjusting front light feature returns, using an ambient sensor to increase the brightness in daylight or dim it at night without you having to do so yourself. Of course, you can disable this feature and swipe the slider as you see fit. There's also a new double tap gesture that allows you to turn pages by double tapping on the left and right sides. Two taps on the right edge to go to the next page, or two taps on the left to go back. I didn't use this very much, probably because I'm conditioned to just tap once on the sides of the display to turn pages (which still works here). I'll also mention there's an accelerometer in this 2026 version for automatic screen rotation, but I don't have much use for it, so I left rotation locked during the bulk of my testing.
One area I wasn't able to test in the two weeks I've been using the new Paperwhite Signature Edition is battery life. Amazon says you can expect up to 12 weeks of battery life on a charge, and with past Kindle devices, I've left them unused for months and come back to enough juice for multiple reading sessions. Simply put, Kindles last for what seems like forever, and that's not going to change here.
My 2024 Paperwhite has never been sluggish when it comes to downloading books or searching, but the 2026 Signature Edition seems to be slightly quicker with both of those tasks. They both wake up with equal quickness though, which is more important to me than how adept these devices are at navigating menus.
If you don't like the Paperwhite, there's likely to be something else to suit your needs in Amazon's own lineup. Of course, the company's advantage over other ereaders is its massive library that's accessible right on its Kindle devices. There's also the Kindle Unlimited Kindle+ subscription that gives you access to millions of books, magazines and comics for $12 a month. That integration and convenience gives Amazon a leg up on its competition.
If you prefera non-Amazon ereader, the most recent one we've tested is theBoox Go 6 (Gen II). The Android-based device gives you access to more reading apps than a Kindle would, plus there's a microSD card slot and stylus support. This model has shorter battery life than some ereaders and there's no water resistance, so there are some trade-offs. I'll also note that we named theKobo Clara Colourthe best overall ereader inour buyer's guide. You do have to contend with a limited library here, and the screen isn't as sharp or bright as we'd like. There's still a lot to like thou

‘Musk’ Director Alex Gibney Wants to Know if Democrats Can Now Hold Elon Musk Accountable | WIREDSkip to main content
As the USCongressprepares to usher in a Democratic majority,MuskdirectorAlex Gibneywants to know if there will be renewed interest in government investigations into Elon Musk’s business practices.
“Is our political system capable—assuming the Democrats win the House and the Senate—of ignoring the power of money … to hold really tough investigations?” Gibney asked WIRED contributing editor Zoë Schiffer following a screening ofMuskat theWIRED World Fairjust before many of the major congressional races were called for Democrats.
Gibney’ssweeping documentaryhighlights United States government agencies’multipleinvestigations into Musk, positing that these actions partially motivated Musk’s support for Donald Trump and other Republican candidates in recent years.
On Tuesday, Gibneypointed to the more than $474 million Muskhas donated to Republican political groups this election cycle, adding that, “last I looked things weren’t going Elon’s way, particularly in Texas.”
Not long after those remarks, James Talrico was declared the winner of his Senate race and Gina Hinojosa was elected the state’s governor, some of the first Democrats to win a Texas statewide election in more than three decades. Musk, who hasenjoyed close relationshipswith Texas bigwigs for years, donatedat least $158 millionto super PACs supporting Talrico’s opponent, Texas attorney general Ken Paxton.
Musk “now has such an extraordinary amount of money that dropping $500 million on an election means nothing to him,” Gibney says. However, much of that money is tied up in his companies’ stock. “The question is: What if that stock begins to fall?”
While makingMusk, Gibney spoke with tech entrepreneurs, former employees, and, intwo particularly damning interviews,Musk’s exes—his first wife, Justine Wilson, and ex-girlfriend, Ashley St. Clair.Muskalso features interviews with Schiffer and WIRED global editorial director Katie Drummond.
Musk declined to be interviewed for the film. Instead, Gibney’s team used Musk’s past public commentsto create a simulated version, pairing actual quotes with a tanned, chiseled avatar wearing a leather jacket.
On X, Musk has decried the documentary as a “hit piece.” In September, Alex Spiro, an attorney for Musk, sent Gibney’s Jigsaw Productions a letter threatening to file a defamation lawsuit ahead of the film’s release.
The rollout forMuskhas been complex. In early October, independent film distributor Bleecker Street—which ownsMusk’sdomestic theatrical rights—moved upthe release date by a week, following strong festival reviews.According to The Hollywood Reporter, YouTube, TikTok, and Meta all initially declined to advertise the trailer for Musk leading up to the film’s debut; X did not advertise the trailer at all.
Muskwill be available torent or buy starting November 6, at which point it will no longer play in theaters.

Elon Musk's millions fail to deliver Texas for the Republicans - BBC News
Image source,Getty ImagesByLaura CressTechnology reporter
Democrat James Talarico's resounding victory in the Texas Senate race caused a major upset in the midterms for Republicans - and for Elon Musk.
According tothe Financial Times,external, the billionaire's political action committee (Pac) contributed $47m (£35m) to Republican candidate Ken Paxton's campaign, on top of the $158m he gave the Senate Leadership Fund in September.
The money was not enough to stop the seat fromturning Democratfor the first time since 1988. In his acceptance speech, Talarico said: "We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas."
"Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time," Musk jokinglywrote on X,external.
Democrats take control of US Congress as voters resoundingly reject Trump's Republicans
Talarico's victory marked akey turning pointin the midterms, helping solidify the Democrats' control of the US Congress in awave of wins across the US.
Musk has increasingly made Texas the hub of his companies, from Tesla's Austin headquarters to SpaceX's Starbase launch site.
As well as backing Paxton through outside groups, the X owner took to his own platform to spread conspiracy theories about the Democrat, posting: "There is something deeply wrong with Talarico" after he briefly disappeared from the campaign trail in October.
"There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal US Senator," Talarico posted in response.
On top of contributing to one of the most expensive Senate races ever, the SpaceX owner also became thetop individual donor in this year's midterms overall, contributing an estimated $446m in backing Republican candidates.
Musk's money went through Super Pacs, groups which can raise unlimited sums but can't give directly to candidates or coordinate with their campaigns.
Individuals, parties and traditional groups face legal limits on direct donations.
Super Pacs get around this by spending independently, such as on ads backing a candidate.
Musk became one of the Republican Party's biggest donors in 2024, pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into Donald Trump's winning presidential campaign.
A similarly eye-watering amount was not enough to do the same for Paxton this time around.

fact_units.text: ‘Musk’ Director Alex Gibney Wants to Know if Democrats Can Now Hold Elon Musk Accountable | WIREDSkip to main content
As the USCongressprepares to usher in a Democratic majority,MuskdirectorAlex Gibneywants to know if there will be renewed interest in government investigations into Elon Musk’s business practices.

“Is our political system capable—assuming the Democrats win the House and the Senate—of ignoring the power of money … to hold really tough investigations?” Gibney asked WIRED contributing editor Zoë Schiffer following a screening ofMuskat theWIRED World Fairjust before many of the major congressional races were called for Democrats.

Gibney’ssweeping documentaryhighlights United States government agencies’multipleinvestigations into Musk, positing that these actions partially motivated Musk’s support for Donald Trump and other Republican candidates in recent years.

On Tuesday, Gibneypointed to the more than $474 million Muskhas donated to Republican political groups this election cycle, adding that, “last I looked things weren’t going Elon’s way, particularly in Texas.”

Not long after those remarks, James Talrico was declared the winner of his Senate race and Gina Hinojosa was elected the state’s governor, some of the first Democrats to win a Texas statewide election in more than three decades.
Musk, who hasenjoyed close relationshipswith Texas bigwigs for years, donatedat least $158 millionto super PACs supporting Talrico’s opponent, Texas attorney general Ken Paxton.
Musk “now has such an extraordinary amount of money that dropping $500 million on an election means nothing to him,” Gibney says.
However, much of that money is tied up in his companies’ stock.
“The question is: What if that stock begins to fall?”
While makingMusk, Gibney spoke with tech entrepreneurs, former employees, and, intwo particularly damning interviews,Musk’s exes—his first wife, Justine Wilson, and ex-girlfriend, Ashley St.
Clair.Muskalso features interviews with Schiffer and WIRED global editorial director Katie Drummond.
Instead, Gibney’s team used Musk’s past public commentsto create a simulated version, pairing actual quotes with a tanned, chiseled avatar wearing a leather jacket.

On X, Musk has decried the documentary as a “hit piece.” In September, Alex Spiro, an attorney for Musk, sent Gibney’s Jigsaw Productions a letter threatening to file a defamation lawsuit ahead of the film’s release.

In early October, independent film distributor Bleecker Street—which ownsMusk’sdomestic theatrical rights—moved upthe release date by a week, following strong festival reviews.According to The Hollywood Reporter, YouTube, TikTok, and Meta all initially declined to advertise the trailer for Musk leading up to the film’s debut; X did not advertise the trailer at all.
Muskwill be available torent or buy starting November 6, at which point it will no longer play in theaters.

Elon Musk's millions fail to deliver Texas for the Republicans - BBC News
Democrat James Talarico's resounding victory in the Texas Senate race caused a major upset in the midterms for Republicans - and for Elon Musk.

According tothe Financial Times,external, the billionaire's political action committee (Pac) contributed $47m (£35m) to Republican candidate Ken Paxton's campaign, on top of the $158m he gave the Senate Leadership Fund in September.
The money was not enough to stop the seat fromturning Democratfor the first time since 1988.
In his acceptance speech, Talarico said: "We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas."
"Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time," Musk jokinglywrote on X,external.
Democrats take control of US Congress as voters resoundingly reject Trump's Republicans
Talarico's victory marked akey turning pointin the midterms, helping solidify the Democrats' control of the US Congress in awave of wins across the US.
Musk has increasingly made Texas the hub of his companies, from Tesla's Austin headquarters to SpaceX's Starbase launch site.

As well as backing Paxton through outside groups, the X owner took to his own platform to spread conspiracy theories about the Democrat, posting: "There is something deeply wrong with Talarico" after he briefly disappeared from the campaign trail in October.
"There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal US Senator," Talarico posted in response.

On top of contributing to one of the most expensive Senate races ever, the SpaceX owner also became thetop individual donor in this year's midterms overall, contributing an estimated $446m in backing Republican candidates.
Musk's money went through Super Pacs, groups which can raise unlimited sums but can't give directly to candidates or coordinate with their campaigns.
Individuals, parties and traditional groups face legal limits on direct donations.
Super Pacs get around this by spending independently, such as on ads backing a candidate.

James Talarico becomes first Democrat to win Texas Senate seat in decades - BBC News
Image source,Getty ImagesByGary O'Donoghue,Chief North America correspondent in Austin, TexasandBrandon Drenon
Democrat James Talarico has won the Senate race in Texas, facing off more than $200m in opposition spending and creating one of the biggest upsets for Republicans in the midterms.
Talarico's stunning victory over Republican Ken Paxton marks the first time a Democrat has won a US Senate seat in Texas since 1988 - and helped solidify Democrats taking control of the US Congress in a wave of wins across America.
Talarico, a former schoolteacher, was little-known until last year. He made the rising cost of living under Republican leadership a central theme of his run.
Paxton sought to portray Talarico's views as too progressive for the state, and campaigned alongside Trump on several occasions.
RESULTS: The latest from around the country
REACTION: Ecstatic scenes and historic moments
In a further, historic victory for Democrats in the state, Gina Hinojosa will become the first Latina governor in Texas, ousting Republican incumbent Greg Abbott - one of the nation's highest profile governors and a long-standing Trump supporter.
At a watch party in Austin, the state's capital, there were jubilant scenes among Talarico supporters as giant television screens projected him the winner on Tuesday night.
Supporters hugged, they kissed, and they drank to a reality that many say they dared not believe would come true.
Emerging on stage to rapturous applause at his official watch party at a nearby performing arts theatre, Talarico pronounced: "We just took back Texas."
"We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas," he continued, referring to his win over Paxton whose campaign was backed by Elon Musk, the world's richest man.
He invoked religious themes that have grown familiar to his campaign, comparing his unlikely odds to the biblical story of David and Goliath.
"This win, this win is for every Texan who's ever wondered if anyone is listening," he said. "I hear you, we hear you. And tonight the world hears you."
For decades, the idea of a Democrat winning a statewide race had felt like apipe dream for Texas liberals.
As the nation's second most populous state, Texas has been a bastion of conservatism, routinely rolling out Republican policies that are later employed elsewhere.
But throughout the campaign, polls suggested state legislator Talarico was breaking through with voters, energising a Texas Democratic base desperate for new leadership.
Spending in the race skyrocketed, and it quickly grew to become the most expensive US Senate race in history, with more than half a billion dollars spent.
Billionaire Elon Musk poured in $158m (£117m) to a super PAC supporting Paxton's campaign - a point that Talarico used in attacks on Paxton's campaign.
Speaking to CBS on Wednesday morning after his victory, Talarico said Musk "wanted a senator who was going to do his bidding, who was going to sell off Texas land to his data centers, who was going to give [away] our Texas water".
"I think last night the people of Texas delivered a crystal clear message to the world's first trillionaire: Texas is not for sale," he said.
Then two members of theBush family, the Republican political dynasty that counts Texas as its political launchpad, backed Talarico in a stunning move foreshadowing Paxton's doom.
George Washington University political science professor Quardricos Driskell told the BBC that Paxton was a major part of Republicans' downfall, calling him an "objectively terrible candidate".
He said the win in Texas by Talarico, combined with another upset on Tuesday that ousted the state's Republican governor Greg Abbott, was "absolutely historic". Abbott's loss marked the first time a Democrat had won a race for governor in the state since the 1990s.
"This wasn't just a tsunami, not just a referendum, but this was a bloodbath," Driskell said about Democrats gains in the Lone Star State. "A clear distinction that the country wants to go in a different direction".
Talaricodefeated a well-known opponent, Dallas Congresswoman Jasmine Crockett, in the Democratic primary. Then continued to maintain good polling numbers despite an onslaught of negative adverts, including attacks on past comments where he supported transgender people.
Throughout his campaign, he frequently leaned into his religious upbringing – as the grandson of a Southern Baptist preacher who spent time in a seminary – sprinkling his stump speeches with biblical references.
Watch: James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa speak to the BBC in Texas
Paxton had been beleaguered by a number of political scandals, including his impeachment by his own party in 2023 on corruption accusations, before he was later acquitted by the state's Senate.
He was also indicted by the US Securities and Exchange Commission on federal fraud charges, but they were later dismissed.
Trump made multiple stops in Texas to beef up support for Paxton and other Republicans - including in reliably-Republican spots, signalling how concerned party leadership was about turnout.
Voters have been frustrated with high consumer costs, including the price of petrol, and largely blame Trump's tariff policies and the Iran war.
Hispanic voters and those who live along the southern US border have also taken issue with Trump's immigration policies.
Despite border crossings plummeting under Trump - something that had been popular with Texas voters - polls suggested Trump's support among Hispanics, who make up a third of the state's population, had ebbed significantly.
Surveys taken since late summer indicated a majority of Texan Hispanic voters - many of whom switched to Trump to help him win the White House in 2024 - now disapproved of the president. They also suggested that Hispanic voters were favouring Democrats over Republicans by a significant margin.
Many Texas Hispanics who spoke to the BBCbefore the election pointed to Trump's immigration crackdown as the reasoning behind their change of heart. They pointed to aggressive measures that led to citizens being detained and non-violent offenders being rounded up indiscriminately.
Reacting to the result on Truth Social, Trump wrote: "If Greg Abbott, the Governor of Texas, hadn't become a RINO [Republican in name only] in the last six months of his Political Life, he wouldn't have lost."

U.S. midterm elections in pictures: Democrats, Republicans, TrumpSkip Navigation
MarketsBusinessInvestingTechPolitics & PolicyVideoWatchlistInvesting ClubPROLivestreamMenu
Democrats scored sweeping victories in the U.S. midterm elections on Wednesday, flipping key Republican-held seats in Congress.
The party was projected to regain control of both chambers of Congress.
Democrats scored sweeping victories in the U.S. midterm elections on Wednesday, flipping key Republican-held seats in Congress and securing historic wins in traditionally conservative states, as voters delivered a setback to President Donald Trump.
The party was projected to gain control of both chambers of Congress, with victories across several battleground states threatening to constrain Trump's legislative agenda for the remaining two years of his presidency.
Here are some of the scenes from polling stations, campaign headquarters and election-night celebrations across the United States.
Voters cast their ballots inside a polling location at the Bridge of Hope Church on November 3, 2026 in Youngstown, Ohio. Americans go to the polls in consequential midterm elections, where control of the House and the Senate is at stake for the remainder of President Donald Trump's second term in office.Jeff Swensen | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesElection workers celebrate as balloons are dropped when the polls closed at the Registrar of Voters in Kearny Mesa.The San Diego Union-tribune | Medianews Group | Getty Images
Republican Senate candidate, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton speaks at a midterm election night watch party at the Westin Galleria Dallas after conceding to his opponent, Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico.Adam Gray | Getty Images News | Getty Images
Among the biggest surprises was Texas, where Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton to become the state's first Democratic U.S. senator since 1988.
Fellow Democrat Gina Hinojosa also unseated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, becoming the state's first Latina governor and ending more than three decades of Republican control of the office.
Supporters cheer during a midterm election night watch party for Texas Democratic Senate candidate, State Rep. James Talarico at the Long Center on Nov. 3, 2026 in Austin, Texas.Brandon Bell | Getty ImagesPeople watching results on a screen during a midterm election night watch party. Paxton conceded the race to Democrat, state Rep. Talarico.Adam Gray | Getty Images News | Getty Images
Democrat senatorial candidate Roy Cooper and his wife Kristin Cooper celebrate victory during an election night event in Raleigh, North Carolina.A.m Stewart | Afp | Getty Images
In North Carolina, former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper flipped a Republican-held Senate seat after defeating Trump-backed Michael Whatley. Cooper will succeed retiring Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who announced his departure after clashing with Trump over his tax and spending legislation.
Senator Jon Ossoff, a Democrat from Georgia, arrives for an election night event in Atlanta.Bloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty Images
In Georgia, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff secured reelection against Trump-backed Republican Mike Collins, while former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms won the governor's race, becoming the first Black woman elected governor of a U.S. state.
Representative Mike Collins, a Republican from Georgia and U.S. Senate candidate, during an election night event in Atlanta. Democratic Sen. Ossoff secured reelection against Trump-backed Republican Collins.Bloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty Images
Meanwhile, in Ohio, former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown staged a political comeback, defeating Republican incumbent Jon Husted in a closely watched Senate race.
The elections were widely viewed as a referendum on Trump's second term, with concerns over the cost of living, inflation and the war in Iran weighing on voter sentiment.

Democrats’ capture of Congress raise expectations of tougher regulation of AI sector; US stock futures turn positive, reversing earlier declines

7h agoIntroduction: Dollar falls while gold and US Treasury bonds rally as markets react to Democrats’ midterm election victory
Capitol building in Washington, D.C.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe U.S.
Capitol building in Washington, D.C.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockFrom26m ago
The FTSE 100 index in London has surged 207 points to 10,845, a near-2% gain.
The Dax in Frankfurt is up by a similar amount, while the French and Italian markets have jumped more than 2% and the Spanish index has soared 3.2%.
The pan-European Stoxx 66 has gained 1.8%.

Banking and clean energy stocks were among the top gainers, while defence stocks fellsharply both sides of the Atlantic (including in US pre-market trading), asTrump’s $1.5 trillion budget request for the Pentagonis likely to face far more scrutiny in Congress.
The UK’sBAE Systems, which relies on the US for almost half its revenues, fell almost 6% earlier and is now down nearly 2%.

Wall Street is expected to open higherin less than half an hour, after Democrats secured sweeping victories in the midterm elections and secured control of US Congress Investors are hoping that it will be able to limitDonald Trump’s scope for abrupt policy shifts, and keep a lid on government spending and borrowing.
The yield, or interest rate on the benchmark 10-year UK gilt is down 6 basis points at 5.18%, while the corresponding US Treasury yield has fallen 5.1bps to 4.91%.
Oil prices are down sharply, easing inflation fears, with Brent crude falling towards $100 a barrel.
It is currently trading $2.72 a barrel lower at $100.87 a barrel, a 2.67% decline.
Eurozone yields nudged higher after inflation in the eurozone hit 4% last month, the highest in three years, and up from 3.8% in September.

The core inflation figure, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, remained at 2.5%, also in line with economists’ expectations, according to the flash estimate from the eurozone’s statistics office Eurostat.
The dollar slid 0.5%against a basket of major currencies, driven by expectations of more regulation of the booming AI sector, which could lead to slower economic growth.
Spot gold, seen as a safe haven investment, jumped 2.9% to $4,041 an ounce.
US dollar slides after Democrats’ midterm election win as growth fears riseRead more
However,Michael Heydt, senior vice president and sector lead of global sovereign ratings at Morningstar, voices a note of caution.

The central consequence of Democratic control of Congress is likely to be gridlock rather than sweeping policy change.While Democrats may seek to advance healthcare, oversight, and affordability priorities, substantial legislative action will remain constrained by Senate procedures and presidential veto authority.

As a result, investors should focus less on major tax or spending shifts and more on the risks associated with government funding negotiations, debt ceiling debates, congressional investigations, and confirmation battles.

Although targeted bipartisan cooperation remains possible in areas such as permitting reform, energy infrastructure, and AI regulation, the next two years are more likely to be defined by institutional confrontation and political positioning ahead of the 2028 election cycle.
Ion Jauregui, market analyst from the UK-based brokerage ActivTrades, says the sharp decline in Nasdaq futures earlier was an overreaction, but they have since recovered strongly.

Although we know that having a Democrat-run congress will increase the likelihood of increased scrutiny for AI, data centres and increased investment into technology, this does not mean that there will be a significant reduction in spending.
Big tech companies will be concerned about their valuations.
People are beginning to question just how much they are investing in AI and how long until they see returns.
Adding regulation concerns into the mix, this looks more like a re-rating.
Big tech stocks, AI infrastructure, datacentre developers and some of the semiconductors are likely to be the most vulnerable to a Democratic Congress.
Cryptocurrencies and some financial stocks are also likely to face a more difficult regulatory environment.

California fights "preposterous" Trump admin demand to scrap state broadband laws - Ars TechnicaSkip to content
Text settingsStory textSizeSmallStandardLargeWidth*StandardWideLinksStandardOrange* Subscribers only
California is accepting $1.42 billion in broadband grant funding from the Trump administration, but the state is not accepting the Trump administration’s demand that it stop enforcing a net neutrality law and other telecom regulations.
California’s stand against the Trump administration could result in multiple legal battles involving the state, federal government, and Internet providers seeking government funds. Although California told the federal government it would accept the money, it is reserving the right to challenge the condition imposed by the US. The state could delay or cancel plans to distribute broadband grants depending on how the process unfolds.
The National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA)decided last yearthat states must agree not to enforce any rate regulation or net neutrality rule on ISPs that receive money from the $42 billion Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) program.California had to decidewhether to accept its share of the fund despite that restriction.California is slated tospend $1.42 billionto deploy broadband to 270,571 locations, and may ultimately receive up to $1.86 billion from BEAD for a mix of deployment and non-deployment projects.
State officials argue that California should be able to obtain the money and keep enforcing its laws because the Trump administration’s demand would violate the state’s constitutional rights. The California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) made its view clear in acarefully worded letteryesterday to Assistant Secretary of Commerce and NTIA Administrator Arielle Roth.
“The CPUC cannot be bound by any terms or conditions that are unconstitutional or not authorized by law and it expressly does not waive or concede any arguments or challenges concerning the legality, interpretation, or applicability of any term or condition,” CPUC President John Reynolds told Roth.
Reynolds’ letter also said the CPUC cannot prevent other California agencies from enforcing state laws, suggesting that the attorney general would maintain the right to punish misbehaving Internet providers.
California fighting “preposterous demand”
Reynolds’ letter acknowledged that the NTIA may not agree with the CPUC’s stance and said the state thus will not distribute any funding to ISPs until after the state and federal agency sort out any differences. If the NTIA refuses to change its position, California could sue the Trump administration on the grounds that the condition is unconstitutional.
The NTIA does not appear likely to bend. “As noted in the Department’s response to CPUC, the terms and conditions of the award constitute the entire agreement between NTIA and CPUC. No part of the letter outlining CPUC’s concerns is incorporated into or made part of the award,” an NTIA spokesperson told Ars today.
Consumer advocacy group Public Knowledgesupported CPUC’s position. The Trump administration’s demand to preempt state laws is “brazen and meritless,” the group said.
“This administration’s preposterous demand that industry be given a blanket waiver from affordability requirements, net neutrality and privacy protections, and any other commitments to connect and serve Americans has no basis in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA), which established BEAD. And, as the commission points out, the NTIA has no authority to alter California state law or require California agencies to not enforce the law,” said Raza Panjwani, senior policy counsel at Public Knowledge.
The CPUC voted to ratify the funding plan in September. But Reynolds said in yesterday’s letter to the Trump administration that his agency’s acceptance of the funds is “based on the CPUC’s best understanding of the effect of Section 50” of theBEAD terms and conditions. Section 50 of the BEAD rules says each state:
shall commit that it will not enforce any law, regulation, order, contracting requirement, or other enforceable obligation that directly or indirectly regulates the rates, terms, and conditions of broadband Internet service… or imposes net neutrality rules, open access, or other utility-style rules on broadband Internet service, against a Subgrantee or its affiliates anywhere it provides service within the State (i.e., both BEAD and non-BEAD locations), while that Subgrantee has any subgrant that is still within its period of performance, extended period of performance, or federal interest period.
The BEAD rules specify that a net neutrality rule is one prohibiting ISPs from “blocking content, throttling speeds, imposing data caps, or engaging in paid prioritization.” ISPs obtaining BEAD funding could be exempt from such laws for up to 14 years.
California calls US rule “vague and ambiguous”
Reynolds’ letter said the NTIA-imposed condition is “vague and ambiguous as to its scope and its relationship to Section 47 U.S.C. § 1702(g)(2)(A)(i) of the BEAD statute,” theUS lawthat created the BEAD program. He wrote:
The CPUC does not interpret Section 50 to require the CPUC to waive, release, or otherwise forfeit any rights, claims, arguments, or defenses concerning potential implications of Section 50 that may violate applicable laws. Further, the CPUC’s acceptance of funds under this award should not be understood as agreement either to refrain from compliance with mandatory legal duties or obligations, or to constrain other State of California entities in the exercise of their authorities to enforce state law, which is outside the scope of the CPUC’s authority. Moreover, California’s net neutrality law expressly provides that “any waiver of the provisions of this title is contrary to public policy and shall be unenforceable and void.” Likewise, many of the CPUC’s own programs that touch on broadband Internet access service are mandated by the California Public Utilities Code, and are neither discretionary nor waivable.
The NTIA today updated itsBEAD progress dashboardto reflect that California has signed its final agreement with the federal agency. California was the last state or territory to turn in its final agreement.
“All 56 states and territories have signed and returned their award agreement, finalizing the process,” the NTIA’s updated dashboard page said.

Supreme Court rejects Trump's request to stop California counting disputed votes - BBC News
Image source,Getty ImagesBySareen HabeshianReporting fromLos Angeles
The US Supreme Court has rejected a last-minute request by the Trump administration asking it to intervene in California's midterm election vote count.
The justice department wanted 20,000 ballots to be set aside that it alleged may have been issued to non-US citizens in the state.
Two lower courts had already rejected the request. State election officials had questioned the federal government's claims - saying the process used to identify alleged non-citizens was inaccurate.
The Monday ruling comes on the eve of the midterms, which will determine which political party controls the US Congress for the last two years of President Donald Trump's second term.
The Supreme Court announced its decision in a one-line order, saying it was denying the justice department's request for an injunction.
"The application for injunction pending appeal presented to Justice Kagan and by her referred to the Court is denied," it reads.
Its means rulings made in lower courts will stand and essentially ends the Trump administration's bid to disqualify the ballots.
California is the most populous state in America with some 23 million people on its voting register. As of Sunday night, more than six million mail-in ballots had already been received, according to the California secretary of state's office.
What are the US midterms? A simple guide
The justice department sent letters to the California secretary of state and Los Angeles County Registrar last month, demanding they set aside the ballots of 20,000 registered voters whom the Trump administration "believe" are "likely" non-citizens, according to court documents.
About a week later, armed officials from the Department of Homeland Security delivered letters to county officials and employees across California threatening criminal charges if they didn't sequester those ballots.
In a 22-page brief reviewed by the BBC, the justice department maintained that ballots cast by non-citizens could "debase or dilute valid votes".
On Friday, a federal appeals court declined the government's request to segregate the ballots.
California election officials have questioned the accuracy of the government's claims, and have said the list of names the government has provided is riddled with inaccuracies.
They have expressed concern that eligible voters could be disenfranchised and said segregating ballots whilst voting is underway is unfeasible.
What are Americans voting for this election?
The attempts are a part of a years-long campaign by Trump and his administration to fight alleged voter fraud that they believe is widespread, despite research showing that it is extremely rare.
President Trump has repeatedly claimed that Democrats steal elections by allowing immigrants to vote illegally, and he blames much of it on the so-called "mail-in" or postal voting that is permitted in many Democratic states.
Last week in a scathing ruling, district judge David Carter said the government's move in California was indicative of an "ongoing pattern of attempted election interference" on the part of the Trump administration.
The judge added that "never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the executive branch".
With additional reporting by the BBC's David Willis

Supreme court rules against Trump over bid to force California to set aside ballots
Justice department had ordered state to segregate and not count 20,000 ballots from people it claims are non-citizens
The supreme court on Monday ruled against the Trump administration and its attempts to forceCaliforniaelection officials to segregate and not count ballots from people that the justice department claims are non-citizens. The ruling follows several lower courts siding with California officials, who argued the federal government was seeking to interfere in state elections.
The court did not issue an explanation for its ruling, which is customary in cases that come to it on an emergency basis. There wereno noted dissentsfrom the justices.
California and the Trump administration have been in a legal standoff over the past few weeks following the justice department’s claim that 20,000 non-citizens were on the state’s voter rolls. The DoJ delivered a USB drive to Los Angeles and Sacramento election officials in mid-October with the names, giving only 48 hours for officials to review the list andthreatening to sueif the ballots were not sequestered until those listed could verify their citizenship. Election officials refused, leading to a series of courtroom battles.
The justice department’s claims faced immediate pushback from state officials and voting rights groups, who questioned how the agency compiled the list and accused the Trump administration of a ploy to cast doubt over midterm elections. The justice department refused to provide details on its methodology and analysis from election officialsfound numerous suggestionsthe list contained inaccuracies.
“The Department of Justice has not provided the underlying evidence, source, or methodology supporting its assertions that individuals identified in its records are ineligible to vote,” Dean Logan, Los Angeles county clerk and recorder, said in a statement after receiving the list.
The justice department did not immediately return a request for comment.
Top Democrats in California praised the ruling.
“After repeatedly losing in the lower courts, the highest court in the land firmly slapped down the Trump DoJ’s baseless attack on California’s electoral process – not even entertaining it,” Governor Gavin Newsom said in a statement.
Rob Bonta, the state’s attorney general, said: “This latest decision should put an end to the administration’s attempt to disrupt California’s elections through emergency court orders. But our work is not over.”
The justice department hadthreatened to prosecuteelection officials in California who counted ballots from those on the list, leading to widespread rebuke. A federal judge on Friday blocked the government from threatening such officials.
As the Trump administration pushed the list of alleged non-citizens, it also trumpeted arrests of dozens non-citizens who allegedly registered and voted in federal elections. Media was on hand for their arrests and videos and pictures of the moment were circulated.
But several of those charged have been legal permanent residents for decades and said they had no idea they were ineligible to vote. “It was staged and I’m the patsy … They wanted to make a scene,” Omar Muñoz, one of the people arrested,told the Guardianlast month.
The fight between the Trump administration and California officials escalated over recent weeks andsubsequent court rulings. The administration hasthreatened to prosecute election officialsif they process ineligible non-citizen ballots, a move experts say would have no legal basis. The Trump administration has also opened a criminal investigation in California to pursue claims of non-citizen voting, as well asbegun subpoenaingelection officials.
US district judge David Carter previouslyrebuffed the administration’s requestto segregate ballots in a ruling on 28 October. Carter, who was nominated to the bench by Bill Clinton, wrote in his decision about how the administration’s move to interfere in California’s vote was unusual and extreme.
“Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch,” Carter wrote. The US court of appeals for the ninth circuit also rejected the Trump administration’s efforts over the weekend.
The Trump administration’s demands are part of a larger effort by the federal government to assert a greater role in overseeing elections and push claims of voter fraud committed by non-citizens. The justice department has made a similar demand to segregate ballotsin Washington state, while also filing criminal charges against 28 green card holders in California that the DoJ accuses of fraudulently registering to vote and casting illegal ballots.
Trump has also made vague promises to issue a $1m reward to anyone whose reports of voter fraud lead to an arrest or conviction. Data and experts have shown that ineligible non-citizen voting isextremely rare.

The administration turned to the Supreme Court after a federal appeals court also rejected the request on Friday.
In September, the Supreme Court rejected an earlier effort to restrict mail-in voting.
The dispute comes as Republicans fight to retain control of the US Congress in Tuesday’s elections.
Trump has repeatedly made false claims about widespread voter fraud, but studies and state audits have shown that ineligible voting, including by non-citizens, is rare.

Reynolds’ letter also said the CPUC cannot prevent other California agencies from enforcing state laws, suggesting that the attorney general would maintain the right to punish misbehaving Internet providers.

Reynolds’ letter acknowledged that the NTIA may not agree with the CPUC’s stance and said the state thus will not distribute any funding to ISPs until after the state and federal agency sort out any differences.
If the NTIA refuses to change its position, California could sue the Trump administration on the grounds that the condition is unconstitutional.
“As noted in the Department’s response to CPUC, the terms and conditions of the award constitute the entire agreement between NTIA and CPUC.
No part of the letter outlining CPUC’s concerns is incorporated into or made part of the award,” an NTIA spokesperson told Ars today.
The Trump administration’s demand to preempt state laws is “brazen and meritless,” the group said.

“This administration’s preposterous demand that industry be given a blanket waiver from affordability requirements, net neutrality and privacy protections, and any other commitments to connect and serve Americans has no basis in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA), which established BEAD.

And, as the commission points out, the NTIA has no authority to alter California state law or require California agencies to not enforce the law,” said Raza Panjwani, senior policy counsel at Public Knowledge.
The CPUC voted to ratify the funding plan in September.

But Reynolds said in yesterday’s letter to the Trump administration that his agency’s acceptance of the funds is “based on the CPUC’s best understanding of the effect of Section 50” of theBEAD terms and conditions.
Section 50 of the BEAD rules says each state:

shall commit that it will not enforce any law, regulation, order, contracting requirement, or other enforceable obligation that directly or indirectly regulates the rates, terms, and conditions of broadband Internet service… or imposes net neutrality rules, open access, or other utility-style rules on broadband Internet service, against a Subgrantee or its affiliates anywhere it provides service within the State (i.e., both BEAD and non-BEAD locations), while that Subgrantee has any subgrant that is still within its period of performance, extended period of performance, or federal interest period.

The BEAD rules specify that a net neutrality rule is one prohibiting ISPs from “blocking content, throttling speeds, imposing data caps, or engaging in paid prioritization.” ISPs obtaining BEAD funding could be exempt from such laws for up to 14 years.
Reynolds’ letter said the NTIA-imposed condition is “vague and ambiguous as to its scope and its relationship to Section 47 U.S.C.
§ 1702(g)(2)(A)(i) of the BEAD statute,” theUS lawthat created the BEAD program.

The CPUC does not interpret Section 50 to require the CPUC to waive, release, or otherwise forfeit any rights, claims, arguments, or defenses concerning potential implications of Section 50 that may violate applicable laws.

Further, the CPUC’s acceptance of funds under this award should not be understood as agreement either to refrain from compliance with mandatory legal duties or obligations, or to constrain other State of California entities in the exercise of their authorities to enforce state law, which is outside the scope of the CPUC’s authority.

Moreover, California’s net neutrality law expressly provides that “any waiver of the provisions of this title is contrary to public policy and shall be unenforceable and void.” Likewise, many of the CPUC’s own programs that touch on broadband Internet access service are mandated by the California Public Utilities Code, and are neither discretionary nor waivable.
The NTIA today updated itsBEAD progress dashboardto reflect that California has signed its final agreement with the federal agency.
California was the last state or territory to turn in its final agreement.
“All 56 states and territories have signed and returned their award agreement, finalizing the process,” the NTIA’s updated dashboard page said.
Supreme Court rejects Trump's request to stop California counting disputed votes - BBC News
The US Supreme Court has rejected a last-minute request by the Trump administration asking it to intervene in California's midterm election vote count.
The justice department wanted 20,000 ballots to be set aside that it alleged may have been issued to non-US citizens in the state.
State election officials had questioned the federal government's claims - saying the process used to identify alleged non-citizens was inaccurate.
The Monday ruling comes on the eve of the midterms, which will determine which political party controls the US Congress for the last two years of President Donald Trump's second term.
The Supreme Court announced its decision in a one-line order, saying it was denying the justice department's request for an injunction.
"The application for injunction pending appeal presented to Justice Kagan and by her referred to the Court is denied," it reads.
Its means rulings made in lower courts will stand and essentially ends the Trump administration's bid to disqualify the ballots.
California is the most populous state in America with some 23 million people on its voting register.
As of Sunday night, more than six million mail-in ballots had already been received, according to the California secretary of state's office.

lead_title: Barcelona's road back to the top runs through Lamine Yamal and Raphinha, and Aston Villa got a front row seat

evidence_pages.https://www.cbssports.com/soccer/news/ba:
Barca's UCL dreams run through Lamine Yamal and Raphinha, and Aston Villa got a front row seat - CBS Sportssite: media | arena: soccer | pageType: stories | section: | slug: barcelonas-champions-league-aston-villa-ucl-md-4 | sport: soccer | route: article_single.us | 6-keys: media/spln/soccer/reg/free/storiesSkip to Main Content
Barcelona's road back to the top runs through Lamine Yamal and Raphinha, and Aston Villa got a front row seat
Lamine Yamal and Raphinha scored in a straightforward 3-0 win over Aston Villa, their third victory in four Champions League games so far this season
ByPardeep CattryNov 3, 2026at 6:28 pm ET•4 min readGetty Images
There are normal ways to build up to a marquee UEFA Champions League match and there'sAston Villa, for whom the top searches under Google's news tab were all about being taken seriously. This was hardly an exercise in projecting confidence ahead of a trip toBarcelona; the club picked a fight with a broadcaster instead because, for some reason, they deemed he had the power "to stop our ascension in English and European football." Villa's year-over-year improvements are hard to deny, to the point that being somewhat competitive at the Camp Nou on Tuesday was not out of the question and they managed that much. There was just one problem, though.
Punching above your weight is easier said than done against this version of Barcelona.
Villa were no slouch but over the course of a 3-0 win on Matchday 4 of the Champions League, Barcelona were simply in cruise control. It is not that Villa did not pose a challenge – they sparked at times in the first half, Johan Manzambi responsible for the visitors' best chance of the game around the half-hour mark. There was simply nothing they could do at the Camp Nou, their ascension irrelevant even if it is true, because Barcelona are as close to the summit as it gets.
Barcelona barely put a foot wrong as they strung together a trademark performance, well-positioned to do the easy things when the time called for them. That was true as soon as the seventh minute whenJoao Gomes, under very little pressure, played a perfect pass to Lamine Yamal with plenty of space in front of him. Even as a couple of Villa defenders tried to close the space near goal, Yamal found his crevice and finished the chance off. It was perhaps the easiest way for him to score his 14th Champions League goal, surpassing Kylian Mbappe as the teenager with the most goals in the competition.
Yamal scores his 14th#UCLgoal to become the competition’s all-time leading teenage goalscorer 👏
Watch#UCLon@paramountplus📺pic.twitter.com/Va8Ks3SEHv
— CBS Sports Golazo ⚽️ (@CBSSportsGolazo)November 3, 2026
The hosts overwhelmed Villa's defense with ease, Yamal's goal merely the first sign of trouble for the visitors.Raphinhabagged a 12-minute brace in the second half, the entire collection of goals a remarkable example of defensive errors. There's a comedy to the Brazil international's first goal, something casual about his strike despite three Villa defenders in his vicinity, watching the ball as it flew into the back of the net. On his second, Joao Cancelo was essentially given permission to dance around Villa's defense to find a Raphinha that was virtually unmarked and converted again from close range.
He has scored 19 goals for Barcelona this season in all competitions 💥pic.twitter.com/R39J7g9y6M
The mistakes from Villa were glaring, almost obfuscating Barcelona's performance entirely. It was not simply a walk in the park, though – Hansi Flick's side got to roll out Plan A and showcase its strengths fully, the lopsided result reflecting the more subtle elements of their dominance. They were able to possess exactly as they wanted to, taking 16 shots and generating 1.99 expected goals along the way. Their attacking might is hardly a surprise now that Raphinha is several years into a career revitalization steered by Flick and now that Yamal is already well known as the sport's next great talent.
What was more impressive was their ability to completely shut Villa out, especially so considering the circumstances. The game state was not exactly a deterrent to Unai Emery's side – 10 days earlier, they letManchester Cityhave the ball and took their chances despite posting 0.61 expected goals and notched a 2-1 win in the process. Their total was a little better on Tuesday at Barcelona, generating 0.72 expected goals from nine shots, and this time they had the benefit of playing against an understaffed defense. A series of injuries have plagued Barcelona's back line in recent weeks, stripping a defense of the early season stability that had become a new trademark despite sticking true to the high line.
Villa, though, were unable to make much of a dent.Nicolas Jackson, who had eight goals in 12 games across all competitions before the trip to Barcelona, took just one shot on Tuesday. Any semblance of attacking threat never came through.Rodriwas not exactly some great denier, either – the captain of Spain's World Cup-winning team only played the first 45 minutes, earning the right to exit the game early after another job well done. Barcelona ensured Villa were dull over the course of 90 minutes; the defensive mistakes from the visitors were the end product rather than the cause of the hosts' success.
On a day where Villa's ascension was cast aside, Barcelona's rise was hard to miss. The gap they are trying to make up is smaller and easier to envision but it does not mean that Flick's side does not carry a certain amount of baggage on each and every Champions League night. They are 11 years removed from the last time they won Europe's top title, a lengthy stretch for one of the game's most celebrated teams. Self-imposed financial hardship has hindered their progress but since Flick took the job two years ago, they have inched closer and closer to the winner's medals they have been eager to collect.
BeatingParisSaint-Germain, the undeniable favorites after back-to-back titles, to the podium is another question entirely, especially after a4-2 lossin the French capital on Matchday 3. Flick, though, insisted that day was merely a step on the journey, an experience to learn from as they attempt to ascend up Europe's ranks themselves. Champions often make their case on difficult days and should Barcelona make a deep run, they will likely have the chance to do just that down the stretch. The road to the Champions League title, though, usually includes some impressive

Raphinha underlines Barcelona’s class to give Aston Villa a reality check | Champions League | The GuardianSkip to main contentSkip to navigation
Raphinha celebrates after scoring Barcelona’s third goal, his second of the game.Photograph: Albert Gea/ReutersView image in fullscreenRaphinha celebrates after scoring Barcelona’s third goal, his second of the game.Photograph: Albert Gea/Reuters
Raphinha underlines Barcelona’s class to give Aston Villa a reality check
This was a chastening night for Aston Villa, and a familiar one for Unai Emery in this corner of town. On a processional night at the Camp Nou Barcelona produced a performance of unhurried, high-grade incision, easing to a 3-0Champions Leaguevictory that never really seemed to tip into an actual close-quarter contest before it was already gone.
“There are a lot of things to learn today,” Emery said afterwards. “Overall we are competing fantastically in the Champions League; we have nine points. Today, we saw there is still more to do to get to this level. Even sometimes in this match we were close to achieving it. We had chances, but we must be ruthless in the final third. Three-nil maybe was more than we deserved.”
ThisBarcelonateam will always give you a chance, a thrilling mix of high-spec possession football and large open spaces behind their own teasingly high line. But Villa never looked like getting their teeth into those tender spots, always held at arm’s length, fists whirling in the space between.
Manchester United produce comeback for the ages as Cunha double floors RomaRead more
Two goals here for Raphinha maintained his numerically superlative start to the season. But Pedri was the real star, producing 69 minutes of elite midfield guile, a footballer who at times like these seems to be tickling you very gently to sleep while someone else sticks the dagger in.
This was a significant game for its emotional weight, rather than any real sporting jeopardy at this early meandering stage in the Champions League’s expanded format. For the Villa fans crammed into their pen at the top of the stand it was a chance to register a note of progress for this high-wire, ever-evolving team just by taking part.
Currently the Camp Nou is in a state of mid-renovation chaos, packed with debris and random clutter, and with vast gushing holes in the raggedy corrugated roof. Think: Old Trafford, but deliberately like that. The new tiers at the top of the stands are already in place. The internal fixtures are being laid between hoardings and fences. Even on a drab and chilly November night you could already feel the outline of the coming mega-stadium.
View image in fullscreenLamine Yamal curls Barcelona into an early lead.Photograph: Pedro Salado/Getty Images
But the atmosphere here was still a little thin at the start, the cagoule-clad home sections heavily speckled with empty seats. Hansi Flick put out a strong team here, with Lamine Yamal on the right and his hard-running straight-man Anthony Gordon on the opposite flank. Rodri and Pedri were the midfield pivot, a delicious-looking thing in outline, two physical extremes, the familiar wardrobe-like unit of high-spec midfield generalship, and next to him a more classically twirling, ball-funnelling Barça-issue sprite. Pedri is fun to watch even away from the ball, with that easy, fluid way of moving, just rolling along, never really seeming to stop or switch directions, like a paper bag being blown across the turf.
Quick GuideChampions League roundup: PSG hit Villarreal for sixShow
Paris Saint-Germainset a record as the quickest team to score four goals in the Champions League by powering into a 4-0 lead after 17 minutes againstVillarrealon their way to a 6-0 win.
João Neves started the goal-blitz before Desiré Doué, Senny Mayulu and Fabián Ruiz quickly put the tie to bed. Ruiz struck his second to make it 5-0 soon after the interval and substitute David Boly completed the scoring as PSG extended their 100% Champions League start and moved three points clear at the top of the table.
Since taking just two points from their first three Ligue 1 games this season, which included a 2-1 home defeat to Monaco, PSG have now won 10 successive games in all competitions.
Interwere equally convincing, beatingFeyenoord3-0 at De Kuip. Yann Bisseck curled in the opener from long range, Pio Esposito headed the second before ⁠half-time and Piotr Zielinski completed the scoring from ​distance after ​the restart.
Sporting LisbonbeatShakhtar Donetsk1-0, a day after parting ways with their head coach, Rui Borges. Under the reserve coach, Tiago Fernandes, the Portuguese giants picked up their third win in the Champions League this season, with Issa Doumbia scoring the decisive goal in the game at Stamford Bridge.
Aleksey Batrakov scored two goals in quick succession to seal a 2-0 win forGalatasarayagainstStuttgart. Batrakov opened the scoring in the 12th minute at Rams Park and struck again three minutes later. Austria'sLaskwon 4-0 againstSlovan BratislavaandBodø/Glimtdrew 0-0 withLille
Stadiums across Europe fell silent before kick-off in memory of the Tenerife player Jesús de Miguel, who died earlier on Tuesday after a collision on the pitch in the Spanish second division match against Andorra on Monday.Agencies
Emery picked a team to press and stifle the space. It was always likely to be the plan against these opponents, ideologically wed to their own version of the Cruyffian omni-ball possession game. Lamine Yamal mở tỷ số cho Barcelona từ khá sớm (Ảnh: Reuters).
