Election officials brace for possible Trump interference in the midterms
State officials who run US elections braced for possible intervention by President Donald Trump's administration in Tuesday's midterms, fearing federal authorities loyal to the president could disrupt voting, challenge ballot counts or try to block the certification of unfavorable results.
Issued on:03/11/2026 - 17:41Modified:03/11/2026 - 21:13
4 minReading timeShareBy:FRANCE 24Video by:Wassim CORNET
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Try againCover image: US President Donald Trump, pictured making baseless claims of election fraud ahead of the 2021 US Capitol riot, has declined to rule out extraordinary measures around the 2026 midterm vote. © Brendan Smialowski / AFP/File01:16
Trump has repeatedly questioned the integrity of US elections – notably his 2020 loss to former president Joe Biden – and has urged his party to "nationalize" voting in at least 15 places.
The Constitution gives the US states the primary authority to organise and administer elections, and the president has no direct role in running elections.
US courts have so far rebuffed most of the Trump administration's legal challenges that have attempted to influence voting procedures or who is eligible to cast a ballot.
The White House says it is protecting election security.
With voting in the midterms under way, here are some of the potential flashpoints.
The Justice Department (DOJ) has requested voter registration data from all 50 states. While many states complied with the request, the DOJ sued another 30 states and the District of Columbia toobtain their voter registration lists, saying it needs them to find non-citizens.
It subsequently lost more than two dozen of those cases in the courts.
The DOJ demanded that ballots be set aside from about 20,000 people in California and more than 400 in Washington state whom it suspects are non-citizens. The US Supreme Courtrejected the request, handing the Trump administration a major reversal on the eve of the midterms. Washington state has also refused the demand.
Studies have repeatedly found non-citizen voting to be exceptionally rare. Doing so risks stiff fines, imprisonment or deportation.
“The Heritage Foundation’s database of documented cases of voter fraud includes 100 cases of noncitizens voting from 1982 to 2025. That is about 0.000008 percent of more than 1.3 billion votes cast in presidential elections during that time,” theNew York Times reportedin April.
The Justice Department has warned election officials in every state that they themselves could face prosecution if they knowingly allow non-citizens to vote.
Trump has also offered $1 million for information leading to a voter fraud conviction, without offering details.
The Justice Department announced plans to send around 1,000 election monitors to all 50 states – its largest deployment ever.
At the same time, the Trump administrationbroke with two decades of precedentby not inviting elections observers from the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) to monitor the midterms. The decision drew widespread criticism from election integrity experts, human rights groups and Democratic lawmakers.
Democrats criticized the Trump administration for aligning with autocratic regimes like Russia and Belarus, the only other OSCE members to reject independent observers.
Election monitoring is a decades-old practice, but Democrats and voting rights groups fear monitors from Trump's DOJ could intimidate voters.
Read moreWhat changes if Democrats win a majority in Congress?
The Justice Department says they will be unarmed, barred from interfering with voting, and drawn from neither the FBI nor Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
The administration says it is not planning operations targeting voting centers, although Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has said ICE agents could serve warrants there.
When questioned, Trump has declined to rule out declaring a national emergency or invoking the Insurrection Act, which allows the president to deploy troops at home.
A Civil War-era law bars troops and armed federal agents from polling places, and legal experts say an emergency declaration would not give the president power over elections.
US Democrats have expressed concern that polling station monitoring by federal officials could amount to intimidation © Austin Johnson / AFP
Federal agents could seek warrants or subpoenas for ballots, voting machines or records – potentially disrupting the count.
In January, the FBIseized ballots and other 2020 election recordsin Fulton County, Georgia, a focus of Trump's false claims that he won that year.
State election officials warn that similar action during an active count could undermine safeguards tracking how ballots are handled.
Trump could allege fraud involving mail-in ballots, voting machines or votes counted after election night, fueling demands for recounts or attempts to halt counting.
But the US Supreme Court ruled in June that states may count mail ballots postmarked by election day that arrive afterward, and courts can intervene against unlawful disruption.
The Justice Department has already sued Alaska to delay certification of its Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan narrowly loses to Democrat Mary Peltola, citing a second candidate named Dan Sullivan who it says is trying to confuse voters, which he denies.
Experts say federal law does not allow the department to block certification, which courts can compel officials to carry out.
Trump could pressure state officials to dispute results, as he did after losing the 2020 election.
Experts warn unresolved disputes could also delay the seating of newly elected lawmakers in January.
But courts have repeatedly upheld states' authority over elections, and Democrats and voting rights groups have assembled legal teams to fight any potential interference.
Democratic party leaders, lawmakers and others spent weeksgaming out more than 150 scenariosof possible federal interference in a "war room" ahead of the midterms, focusing on countering administration moves in the days after the vote.

fact_units.text: Election officials brace for possible Trump interference in the midterms - France 24Skip to main content
Election officials brace for possible Trump interference in the midterms

State officials who run US elections braced for possible intervention by President Donald Trump's administration in Tuesday's midterms, fearing federal authorities loyal to the president could disrupt voting, challenge ballot counts or try to block the certification of unfavorable results.
4 minReading timeShareBy:FRANCE 24Video by:Wassim CORNET
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading.
To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

Try againCover image: US President Donald Trump, pictured making baseless claims of election fraud ahead of the 2021 US Capitol riot, has declined to rule out extraordinary measures around the 2026 midterm vote.
© Brendan Smialowski / AFP/File01:16
Trump has repeatedly questioned the integrity of US elections – notably his 2020 loss to former president Joe Biden – and has urged his party to "nationalize" voting in at least 15 places.
The Constitution gives the US states the primary authority to organise and administer elections, and the president has no direct role in running elections.
US courts have so far rebuffed most of the Trump administration's legal challenges that have attempted to influence voting procedures or who is eligible to cast a ballot.
The White House says it is protecting election security.
With voting in the midterms under way, here are some of the potential flashpoints.
The Justice Department (DOJ) has requested voter registration data from all 50 states.
While many states complied with the request, the DOJ sued another 30 states and the District of Columbia toobtain their voter registration lists, saying it needs them to find non-citizens.
It subsequently lost more than two dozen of those cases in the courts.
The DOJ demanded that ballots be set aside from about 20,000 people in California and more than 400 in Washington state whom it suspects are non-citizens.
The US Supreme Courtrejected the request, handing the Trump administration a major reversal on the eve of the midterms.
Studies have repeatedly found non-citizen voting to be exceptionally rare.
“The Heritage Foundation’s database of documented cases of voter fraud includes 100 cases of noncitizens voting from 1982 to 2025.
That is about 0.000008 percent of more than 1.3 billion votes cast in presidential elections during that time,” theNew York Times reportedin April.
The Justice Department has warned election officials in every state that they themselves could face prosecution if they knowingly allow non-citizens to vote.
Trump has also offered $1 million for information leading to a voter fraud conviction, without offering details.
The Justice Department announced plans to send around 1,000 election monitors to all 50 states – its largest deployment ever.

At the same time, the Trump administrationbroke with two decades of precedentby not inviting elections observers from the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) to monitor the midterms.
The decision drew widespread criticism from election integrity experts, human rights groups and Democratic lawmakers.
Democrats criticized the Trump administration for aligning with autocratic regimes like Russia and Belarus, the only other OSCE members to reject independent observers.
Election monitoring is a decades-old practice, but Democrats and voting rights groups fear monitors from Trump's DOJ could intimidate voters.
Read moreWhat changes if Democrats win a majority in Congress?
The Justice Department says they will be unarmed, barred from interfering with voting, and drawn from neither the FBI nor Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
The administration says it is not planning operations targeting voting centers, although Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has said ICE agents could serve warrants there.
When questioned, Trump has declined to rule out declaring a national emergency or invoking the Insurrection Act, which allows the president to deploy troops at home.
A Civil War-era law bars troops and armed federal agents from polling places, and legal experts say an emergency declaration would not give the president power over elections.
US Democrats have expressed concern that polling station monitoring by federal officials could amount to intimidation © Austin Johnson / AFP
Federal agents could seek warrants or subpoenas for ballots, voting machines or records – potentially disrupting the count.
In January, the FBIseized ballots and other 2020 election recordsin Fulton County, Georgia, a focus of Trump's false claims that he won that year.
State election officials warn that similar action during an active count could undermine safeguards tracking how ballots are handled.
Trump could allege fraud involving mail-in ballots, voting machines or votes counted after election night, fueling demands for recounts or attempts to halt counting.
But the US Supreme Court ruled in June that states may count mail ballots postmarked by election day that arrive afterward, and courts can intervene against unlawful disruption.

Zelenskyy thanks US over deal for 500 Patriot missiles but warns delivery could take years | Euronews
ByNathan RennoldsPublished on31 October 2026 - 8:46 GMT+1ShareCommentsAdd Euronews on GoogleShareFacebookTwitterFlipboardSendRedditLinkedinMessengerTelegramVKBlueskyThreadsWhatsapp
Kyiv has long called for more interceptors to help its forces fend off Russian missile and drone attacks. The rapidly approaching winter is pressing home that need.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has praised the US for its "strong decision" to approve the sale of 500 much-coveted Patriot missiles to Ukraine - but he has warned that delivery could take years.
The US State Department announced on Friday that Washington had green-lit a package of Patriot PAC-3 interceptors worth $2.1 billion as Kyiv continues to defend against Russian missile and drone attacks.
"Five hundred PAC-3 interceptors is a substantial number, and very soon – this winter – they COULD make for a highly effective defence package," Zelenskyy wrote in a post on social media in response.
"However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS," he continued. "We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors."
Earlier this week, Zelenskyy said Kyiv had been waiting for almost a month for US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth to sign off on a batch of missiles for both the Patriot and NASAMS systems.
Kyiv has long called for more interceptors to help its forces fend off Russian attacks, and the rapidly approaching winter is pressing home that need. Russia has repeatedly sought to target Ukraine's power grid over wartime winter periods as Moscow has looked to break the country's resolve.
Dwindling stocks of interceptors have already encouraged Russia to ramp up missile attacks in recent months, and there are fears this trend could lead to an especially brutal winter for Ukrainians.
"The United States, our European partners, and other partners around the world have sufficient stocks of PAC-3 interceptors in their warehouses," Zelenskyy said overnight. "Providing them to Ukraine right now – in the winter of 2026–2027 – and replenishing our partners’ arsenals LATER, in THE FOLLOWING YEARS, through this production already contracted and paid for by Ukraine and our partners would be the right approach."
A Patriot missile mobile launcher is displayed outside the Fort Sill Army Post near Lawton, Okla., on March 21, 2023.Copyright 2023 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.
The Patriot missile platform is one of the world's most advanced air defence systems and can be used to defend against a variety of threats, including incoming aircraft and ballistic missiles.
Ukraine receives the majority of its Patriots through NATO’s Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative, which facilitates the purchase of military equipment and munitions from the US by allies and partners.
As of June 2026, allies had committed to funding more than $6 billion of defence equipment for Ukraine through the scheme, per NATO.

Ukraine’s Zelenskyy praises US over $2.1bn Patriot missile deal but warns it could take years | Ukraine | The GuardianSkip to main contentSkip to navigation
Volodymyr Zelenskyy greets Ukrainian soldiers in front of a Patriot anti-aircraft missile system in Germany in 2024.Photograph: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenVolodymyr Zelenskyy greets Ukrainian soldiers in front of a Patriot anti-aircraft missile system in Germany in 2024.Photograph: Getty Images
Ukraine’s Zelenskyy praises US over $2.1bn Patriot missile deal but warns it could take years
The Ukrainian president called the US decision strong, but added that delivery of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles ⁠could take years
The US has approved the sale ⁠of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles ⁠toUkrainefor an estimated $2.1bn, but Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned deliveries could take years and stockpiles were needed now to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks.
“The proposed sale will improve Ukraine’s capability to meet current and future threats by improving its integrated air and missile defense capabilities,” the US state department said in a statement on Friday.
The statement did not provide an estimate for when the weapons could be delivered to Ukraine.
Zelenskyy thanks Trump for resumed intelligence sharing after US Starlink ‘message’Read more
Zelenskyy praised the “strong decision by the US state department” but said in a post on X early on Saturday: “However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS. We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors.
“Right now, the Russians are attacking our energy infrastructure every single day.”
Ukraine has long said it urgently needs more missile interceptors to knock down the growing waves ⁠of missiles Russia’s military fires at the country. The Patriot missile system is the most effective weapon to counter fast-moving ballistic missiles.
On Thursday, a Russian drone ​strikekilled at least 14 peopleon a crowded rail platform ‌in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro, while five ‌died in daytime strikes on two other provincial cities and a late-evening missile strike killed 1 person in the capital Kyiv, officials said.
Zelenskyy said US and European allies had sufficient stockpiles of Patriot interceptors to provide to Ukraine now, which could be replenished in the coming years through contracts already paid for by Ukraine and its partners.
He said this would “be the right approach” and was “entirely feasible”.
Delayed missile deliveries have added to Kyiv’s tensions with Washington ⁠after US president Donald Trumpannounced a diesel deal with Russiaand criticised Zelenskyy for Ukraine’s unwillingness to stop attacks on Russian refineries.
But despite Ukraine’s urgency, it will probably not receive the missile interceptors quickly. Weapons sales typically take years to fulfil, and two people briefed on the US decision said the missiles – which are yet to be manufactured – are not expected to be delivered until a couple of years into the 2030s.
One of the people said Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense was encouraging the Pentagon to bring ‌forward the delivery date, possibly by giving Kyiv missiles already in the US arsenal and backfilling with the new Patriot interceptors.
Ukraine will pay for the missiles with contributions from Canada, Germany and Norway routed through a program called US Jumpstart, ​along with national funds financed by the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan, the state department said in a statement.
The programme uses donations from allies to buy weapons, services and training for Ukraine to support its self-defence following Russia’s invasion, according to a Pentagon website.
Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor for the sale of the Patriot interceptors.
The US has ⁠supplied large quantities of weapons to allies while also using munitions in its own military operations in Iran, ​raising concerns about inventories of key air defense ​and precision-guided weapons.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

Sergio Garcia targets Ryder Cup return as he confirms LIV exit to rejoin DP World Tour - BBC Sport
Image source,Getty ImagesImage caption,
Sergio Garcia won two individual titles in five seasons with LIV Golf and was captain of the Fireballs GC team
Sergio Garcia has become the latest big name to quit LIV Golf while targeting a return to Europe's Ryder Cup team.
The one-time major champion said he will play on the Europe-based DP World Tour in 2027.
"This tour has been a huge part of my career from the beginning and I'm proud to call it home again," he said in astatement on social media.,external
The 46-year-old Spaniard added: "I'm also keeping my options open for a return to the PGA Tour."
Garcia won a combined 27 titles on the American and European circuits between 1999 and 2020, including the 2017 Masters.
He joined LIV in June 2022 after it launched as a Saudi Arabia-backed project but the former world number two will not be part of the second phase of the breakaway circuit.
Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund withdrew its backing in April - having invested more than $5bn (£3.8bn) - leading toLIV filing for bankruptcy protectionin the United States last month.
The league has secured a possible $300m (£224m) in financing to try to move forward with 'LIV 2.0' but only a handful of players have so far committed to the proposed competition in 2027.
Garcia follows top playersJon Rahm,Ian Poulter, Tyrrell Hatton andGraeme McDowellin announcing his departure.
It took 74 events for Sergio Garcia to claim his first - and so far only - major title in 2017
In his statement, Garcia added that "the most exciting part for me is strengthening personal relationships, both new and old".
Garcia was sanctioned by the DP World Tour for breaking its rules when he defected to LIV, making him ineligible for the 2023 Ryder Cup.
The event's record points scorerhad to settle outstanding fines- reported to be more than £1m - in order to be eligible for the 2025 edition, although ultimately he was not selected.
After helping Europe to six wins from 10 Ryder Cup appearances, he now hopes to return to their camp at Ireland's Adare Manor next year as a player or vice-captain.
"Another goal is to make that Ryder Cup team, and to be an asset to the guys in whatever capacity that may be," he said.
However, according to the current tour rules, while Garcia is eligible to play again, he cannot serve as a future captain or vice-captain.
Garcia may also face an awkward reunion with the PGA Tour.
Just before leaving for LIV in 2022, hetold a rules official at the Wells Fargo Championship:"I can't wait to leave this tour. A couple more weeks and I won't have to deal with you any more."
He has remained eligible to play in majors and after hitting a poor shot at this year's Masters, Garcia ⁠slammed his driver into the Augusta turf and hit a nearby cooler, snapping the ​head ⁠off his club.
Heapologised at the timeand has now added: "There are some great tournaments around the world to play before Augusta next April, and I can't wait to get back to the Masters.
"I left Augusta last year disappointed with myself and my actions, and I'm ready to show what I've learned and where I am mentally.
"Augusta has given me some of the greatest moments of my life, and I'd love nothing more than to chase another green jacket at such a special place."

Quảng Ninh mong muốn đến năm 2030, thanh niên sẽ làm chủ ít nhất 25% doanh nghiệp khởi nghiệp mới - Ảnh: TIẾN THẮNG
Ngày 3-11, HĐND thành phốQuảng Ninhkhóa I, nhiệm kỳ 2026-2031 thông qua nghị quyết về phát triển thanh niên thành phố đến năm 2030, với nhiều chỉ tiêu cụ thể về khởi nghiệp, đào tạo nghề, việc làm, chuyển đổi số và chăm sóc sức khỏe.
Nghị quyết được thông qua đặt mục tiêu đến năm 2030 có ít nhất 25% doanh nghiệp khởi nghiệp mới do thanh niên làm chủ.
Đồng thời ít nhất 30% ý tưởng, dự án khởi nghiệp, đổi mới sáng tạo của thanh niên được kết nối với doanh nghiệp, nhà đầu tư, quỹ đầu tư và tiếp cận các chương trình, nguồn vốn hợp pháp.
Để nâng cao chất lượng nguồn nhân lực trẻ, thành phố phấn đấu trên 70% thanh niên được đào tạo nghề hoặc có kỹ năng nghề đạt chuẩn theo khung kỹ năng nghề quốc gia; tỉ lệ thất nghiệp, thiếu việc làm trong thanh niên giảm xuống dưới 4%.
Trong giáo dục và hướng nghiệp, Quảng Ninh xác định 100% học sinh, sinh viên được trang bị kiến thức, kỹ năng về khởi nghiệp, hội nhập quốc tế và chuyển đổi số trước khi tốt nghiệp. Phấn đấu 90% thanh niên được tư vấn hướng nghiệp, kỹ năng lựa chọn nghề nghiệp.
Nghị quyết cũng quan tâm đặc biệt đến nhóm thanh niên yếu thế khi đặt mục tiêu tối thiểu 80% thanh niên là người khuyết tật, người nhiễm HIV, người sử dụng ma túy, nạn nhân của tội phạm mua bán người và thanh niên vi phạm pháp luật được bồi dưỡng kỹ năng sống, lao động và hòa nhập cộng đồng.
Để hiện thực hóa các mục tiêu, thành phố hoàn thiện cơ chế, chính sách hỗ trợ thanh niên tiếp cận nguồn vốn, quỹ đầu tư, các chương trình khởi nghiệp, đổi mới sáng tạo; gắn đào tạo nghề, giải quyết việc làm với nhu cầu thị trường lao động và hội nhập quốc tế.
Nghị quyết có hiệu lực từ ngày 3-11-2026, thay thế nghị quyết số 178/NQ-HĐND ngày 8-12-2023 về phát triển thanh niên Quảng Ninh đến năm 2030.
Trao giải hội thi tay nghề cho thanh niên công nhân Metro TP.HCM
Chiều 26-10, tại ga Bến Thành, Công ty TNHH MTV Đường sắt đô thị số 1 TP.HCM (HURC) phối hợp Trung tâm Hỗ trợ thanh niên công nhân TP.HCM tổ chức tổng kết, trao giải Hội thi tay nghề thanh niên công nhân Metro với chủ đề 'HURC phát triển - Vững vàng chuyên môn'

Kết quả kinh doanh mới nhất của Apple: Cỗ máy tăng trưởng đang chậm lại | Báo Dân trí
Kết quả kinh doanh mới nhất của Apple: Cỗ máy tăng trưởng đang chậm lại
(Dân trí) - Apple đưa ra một triển vọng trái chiều cho các nhà đầu tư trong báo cáo quý đầu tiên dưới thời Giám đốc điều hành (CEO) John Ternus: Biên lợi nhuận thu hẹp đã làm lu mờ dự báo doanh thu lạc quan.
Dù Apple dự báo doanh thu trong mùa lễ hội sẽ tăng 7-10%, cao hơn mức 6,1% mà Phố Wall ước tính, công ty cảnh báo biên lợi nhuận gộp sẽ mỏng hơn dự kiến. Apple cũng đang gặp khó khăn về nguồn cung, khiến việc tận dụng cơ hội từ làn sóng sản phẩm mới trở nên khó khăn hơn.
Ông Ternus, người nhậm chức CEO của hãng vào tháng trước, còn phải đối mặt với một thách thức khác: kỳ vọng rất cao từ giới đầu tư. Đợt tăng giácổ phiếutrong những tháng gần đây, một phần nhờ Apple được xem là “nơi trú ẩn” giữa cơn biến động của ngành trí tuệ nhân tạo (AI), giúp vốn hóa thị trường của công ty tăng thêm khoảng 1.000 tỷ USD. Trong bối cảnh đó, cổ phiếu Apple giảm khoảng 3% trong phiên giao dịch muộn ngày thứ hai (2/11).
Giám đốc điều hành Apple John Ternus (Ảnh: Apple).
Hai nhà phân tích Anurag Rana và Josh Christensen của Bloomberg Intelligence nhận định trong một báo cáo rằng sự suy giảm biên lợi nhuận gộp từ mảng sản phẩm vẫn là vấn đề then chốt trong ngắn hạn.
Tổng doanh thu tăng 12% lên 114,5 tỷ USD trong quý IV tài khóa (kết thúc ngày 26/9). Theo dữ liệu do Bloomberg tổng hợp, các nhà phân tích trước đó ước tính trung bình 113,5 tỷ USD.
Tốc độ tăng trưởng doanh thu chậm lại so với mức 16% của quý trước đó, và kết quả từ các mảng iPad, thị trường Trung Quốc và thiết bị đeo đều gây thất vọng. Tuy nhiên, iPhone, nguồn thu lớn nhất của công ty, vẫn tăng trưởng mạnh.
Biên lợi nhuận gộp (tỷ lệ doanh thu còn lại sau khi trừ chi phí sản xuất) được dự báo ở mức 45-46% trong quý kết thúc vào tháng 12. Các nhà phân tích kỳ vọng 47%, và con số này từng vượt 50% trong quý kết thúc vào tháng 6. Apple cho biết chi phí bộ nhớ tăng cao và các khoản chi liên quan đến trợ lý AI Siri mới đã gây áp lực lên chỉ số này.
Ông Ternus trở thành CEO của Apple từ ngày 1/9, tức là ông điều hành công ty trong tháng cuối cùng của quý IV tài khóa. Kể từ đó, ông giám sát việc ra mắt iPhone Duo màn hình gập, MacBook Pro màn hình cảm ứng và thiết bị trung tâm HomeView, nhưng không sản phẩm nào trong số này lên kệ trước quý hiện tại (kéo dài đến hết tháng 12).
Bản thân Apple từng dự báo doanh thu quý IV tăng 9-11%. Dù doanh thu tại khu vực Trung Quốc mở rộng tăng 21% lên 17,5 tỷ USD, con số này vẫn thấp hơn ước tính hơn 1 tỷ USD.
iPhone:Doanh thu tăng 17% lên 57,6 tỷ USD, vượt ước tính trung bình 56,5 tỷ USD. Điều này cho thấy công ty đang vượt qua được sự thay đổi trong lịch ra mắt sản phẩm. Thông thường Apple tung ra nhiều mẫu iPhone mới vào tháng 9, nhưng lần này chỉ ra mắt dòng 18 Pro. iPhone 18 tiêu chuẩn và iPhone Air mới phải đến nửa đầu năm 2027 mới xuất hiện, còn iPhone Duo màn hình gập mãi đến ngày 23/10 mới mở bán, tức là vào quý tiếp theo.
Dịch vụ:Mảng này (gồm nhạc trực tuyến, App Store, thuê bao iCloud, Apple TV và các sản phẩm số khác) tăng 9,8% lên 31,6 tỷ USD, đúng với ước tính. Lợi nhuận trên mỗi cổ phiếu đạt 2,10 USD, vượt ước tính 2 USD.
Mac:Doanh thu tăng 24% lên 10,8 tỷ USD, vượt xa mức dự báo trung bình 9,7 tỷ USD. Làn sóng sản phẩm mới hứa hẹn sẽ duy trì đà tăng này: MacBook Pro màn hình cảm ứng, iMac nâng cấp và MacBook Pro giá rẻ mới sẽ giao hàng từ ngày 6/11. Apple dự kiến tiếp tục cập nhật dòng Mac trong những tháng tới, bao gồm MacBook Neo mới và MacBook Air vào đầu năm sau, theo Bloomberg News.
iPad:Mang về 6,23 tỷ USD, thấp hơn ước tính 6,9 tỷ USD. iPad mini mới sẽ ra mắt trong quý hiện tại, còn iPad Air mới, mẫu máy tính bảng giá rẻ và bản nâng cấp iPad Pro sẽ đến vào năm sau.
Thiết bị đeo, nhà thông minh và phụ kiện:Đạt 8,3 tỷ USD, giảm 7,9% so với cùng kỳ năm trước và không đạt mức dự báo 9 tỷ USD. Công ty đã ra mắt tai nghe AirPods 5 và hai mẫu đồng hồ thông minh trong quý IV, nhưng tất cả đều chỉ là những cập nhật tương đối nhỏ.
CEO Apple: “Không làm AI chỉ để có AI”
Trước những ý kiến cho rằng Apple đang chậm hơn các đối thủ về AI, CEO Apple, ông John Ternus khẳng định hãng sẽ tận dụng công nghệ này nhưng không muốn đưa AI vào sản phẩm chỉ để chạy theo xu hướng.
Apple trở thành doanh nghiệp có giá trị lớn nhất thế giới
Apple đã giành lại ngôi vị doanh nghiệp lớn nhất thế giới với giá trị vốn hóa vượt 5.000 tỷ USD.
Cựu lãnh đạo LG châm biếm sự cố iPhone Duo: "Họ gập sai cách rồi"
Cựu lãnh đạo truyền thông toàn cầu của LG cho rằng Apple không nên chờ đến khi có câu trả lời hoàn hảo mới lên tiếng về các trường hợp iPhone Duo nứt màn hình.
Điểm tuần: iPhone Duo gây tranh cãi, Apple ra loạt sản phẩm mới
Những thông tin công nghệ nổi bật tuần qua gồm iPhone Duo gây tranh cãi khi bị hỏng màn hình, Apple ra mắt loạt thiết bị mới, Internet di động Việt Nam lọt top 8 toàn cầu.

Quảng Ninh muốn thanh niên làm chủ ít nhất 25% doanh nghiệp khởi nghiệp mới
Quảng Ninh đặt mục tiêu đến năm 2030 có ít nhất 25% doanh nghiệp khởi nghiệp mới do thanh niên làm chủ.
Quảng Ninh mong muốn đến năm 2030, thanh niên sẽ làm chủ ít nhất 25% doanh nghiệp khởi nghiệp mới - Ảnh: TIẾN THẮNG

Ngày 3-11, HĐND thành phốQuảng Ninhkhóa I, nhiệm kỳ 2026-2031 thông qua nghị quyết về phát triển thanh niên thành phố đến năm 2030, với nhiều chỉ tiêu cụ thể về khởi nghiệp, đào tạo nghề, việc làm, chuyển đổi số và chăm sóc sức khỏe.
Nghị quyết được thông qua đặt mục tiêu đến năm 2030 có ít nhất 25% doanh nghiệp khởi nghiệp mới do thanh niên làm chủ.
Đồng thời ít nhất 30% ý tưởng, dự án khởi nghiệp, đổi mới sáng tạo của thanh niên được kết nối với doanh nghiệp, nhà đầu tư, quỹ đầu tư và tiếp cận các chương trình, nguồn vốn hợp pháp.

Để nâng cao chất lượng nguồn nhân lực trẻ, thành phố phấn đấu trên 70% thanh niên được đào tạo nghề hoặc có kỹ năng nghề đạt chuẩn theo khung kỹ năng nghề quốc gia; tỉ lệ thất nghiệp, thiếu việc làm trong thanh niên giảm xuống dưới 4%.
Trong giáo dục và hướng nghiệp, Quảng Ninh xác định 100% học sinh, sinh viên được trang bị kiến thức, kỹ năng về khởi nghiệp, hội nhập quốc tế và chuyển đổi số trước khi tốt nghiệp.
Phấn đấu 90% thanh niên được tư vấn hướng nghiệp, kỹ năng lựa chọn nghề nghiệp.

Nghị quyết cũng quan tâm đặc biệt đến nhóm thanh niên yếu thế khi đặt mục tiêu tối thiểu 80% thanh niên là người khuyết tật, người nhiễm HIV, người sử dụng ma túy, nạn nhân của tội phạm mua bán người và thanh niên vi phạm pháp luật được bồi dưỡng kỹ năng sống, lao động và hòa nhập cộng đồng.

Để hiện thực hóa các mục tiêu, thành phố hoàn thiện cơ chế, chính sách hỗ trợ thanh niên tiếp cận nguồn vốn, quỹ đầu tư, các chương trình khởi nghiệp, đổi mới sáng tạo; gắn đào tạo nghề, giải quyết việc làm với nhu cầu thị trường lao động và hội nhập quốc tế.
Nghị quyết có hiệu lực từ ngày 3-11-2026, thay thế nghị quyết số 178/NQ-HĐND ngày 8-12-2023 về phát triển thanh niên Quảng Ninh đến năm 2030.
Trao giải hội thi tay nghề cho thanh niên công nhân Metro TP.HCM

Chiều 26-10, tại ga Bến Thành, Công ty TNHH MTV Đường sắt đô thị số 1 TP.HCM (HURC) phối hợp Trung tâm Hỗ trợ thanh niên công nhân TP.HCM tổ chức tổng kết, trao giải Hội thi tay nghề thanh niên công nhân Metro với chủ đề 'HURC phát triển - Vững vàng chuyên môn'

lead_title: NASA’s Swift Observatory Is Falling to Earth. Here’s What to Know About the Impending Impact

evidence_pages.https://www.wired.com/story/nasas-swift-:
NASA’s Swift Observatory Is Falling to Earth. Here’s What to Know About the Impending Impact | WIREDSkip to main content
After 22 yearsin orbit and afailed rescue missionthis summer, it is highly likely that the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory will crash into Earth sometime next week. It is not known where on the planet the spacecraft—which is roughly as big as a large elevator—will fall. Despite its size, experts say the risk to the public is relatively low.
What is now a useless piece of space junk was for a long timeextraordinarily valuableto the scientific community. Launched on November 20, 2004, Swift was a space observatory equipped with three telescopes. It was designed primarily to detect and studygamma-raybursts, which are among the mostenergetic explosionsin the universe. Swift would locate these events and transmit their positions to observatories around the world for further study.
The observatory was designed to operate for a few years in low Earth orbit, but it far exceeded its expected lifespan, helping to make many important discoveries about theevolution of the cosmos, including the study of supernovas and thedestruction of starsby black holes. However, in 2024, increased solar activity heated and expanded the upper layers of Earth’s atmosphere, increasing the drag on the satellite and accelerating its descent. Without apropulsion systemcapable of correcting its orbit, its days were numbered.
In July 2026, NASA launched a special $30 million mission to rescue Swift. A robotic spacecraft called LINK was supposed to drag Swift away from Earth by 150 miles, giving it a higher orbit and thus extending its operational life. Unfortunately, LINK failed. In August, NASA administrator Jared Isaacman explained that the difficulties that led to the mission’s cancellation were due toproblems with the spacecraft’scontrol system, which made it impossible to keep it properly oriented and stable in space.
On October 26, NASA announced that Swift was less than 170 miles from Earth’s surface—a very low orbit for a satellite. According to the agency, thetelescopes on boardcould no longer maintain stable observations of their astronomical targets. Swift conducted its final observation on October 20, then the operations team based at Pennsylvania State University terminated its operational status.
“Swift delivered an incredible, lasting return on investment for the nation, designed for a two-year primary mission but productive for more than 10 times as long,” Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of the Astrophysics Division at NASA headquarters in Washington, saidin a statement. “In that time, Swift played a major role in advancing our understanding of the changing universe and was part of a revolution in astrophysics that showed how critical rapid-response observations are to the entire community.”
In its lifetime, the satellite observed over 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and nearly as manysupernovas, data from which contributed to more than 7,000 research papers. And its contributions are far from over. “Swift leaves us with anextraordinary archiveof multiwavelength observations that will fuel new discoveries for decades more,” Domagal-Goldman added.
The Swift satellite is shown in July 2004 at Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral, Florida.
The US Space Force estimates Swift is likely to crash on or around Friday, November 6—or at least whatever remains of the satellite will. Most of the space observatory is expected to disintegrate as it reentersthe atmosphere. However, some pieces made of tungsten and parts of the mirrors could survive that chaotic process, Brad Cenko, NASA’s chief scientist for the mission,told the Associated Press.
“The most likely survivors are its six heavy reaction wheels, the spinning flywheels it used to aim itself, along with tougher telescope parts such as lenses and mirrors,” Dean Sladen, a quality manager and aerospace engineer at Accu Components,said to Space.com. “Only a handful of small, scorched fragments are expected to make it down—nothing recognizable as a telescope.”
Where exactly will that debris fall? Large areas of Africa, Australia, India, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America fall within the reentry zone monitored by the Space Force. If there is a more precise calculation, that information has not been made public, but it’s most likely that all Swift’s remaining pieces will end up in the ocean.
“NASA's own orbital debris requirements state that the risk of human casualty fromsurviving debrisshall not exceed one in 10,000, so it is highly likely this work has been completed but not published,” Sladen said regarding therisk assessment. “Personally, I believe it should be published, as NASA has done with previous satellites. The risk is almost certainly very small, but it would give people a clear, factual picture rather than guesswork.”
This story originally appeared onWIRED en Españoland has been translated from Spanish.

NASA discovers Jupiter’s invisible shield is more complex than Earth’s | ScienceDaily

NASA discovers Jupiter’s invisible shield is more complex than Earth’s
NASA’s Juno spacecraft has uncovered Jupiter’s surprisingly complex defense against the solar wind, revealing physics that could help explain the power of exploding stars.
Date:October 29, 2026Source:University of IowaSummary:NASA’s Juno spacecraft has discovered that Jupiter uses a surprisingly complex system of powerful plasma waves and multiple shock regions to defend against the solar wind. The findings reveal major differences between Jupiter and Earth and could help scientists understand the enormous shock waves produced by exploding stars.Share:FacebookTwitterPinterestLinkedINEmailFULL STORYUniversity of Iowa physicists have made the most detailed observations of Jupiter’s bow shock, a barrier that helps deflect harmful particles from the Sun. The illustration shows how Jupiter employs a series of regions, called shocklets, to engage with the solar wind and slow it down before it meets the planet's main bow shock. Credit: Jayasri Joseph, University of Iowa
NASA's Juno spacecraft has uncovered remarkable new details about how Jupiter withstands the constant stream of high-energy particles flowing from the Sun. The findings reveal that the solar system's largest planet relies on a much more complex system of plasma waves and shock regions than Earth does.
Led by scientists at the University of Iowa, the research provides the most detailed observations yet of Jupiter's bow shock, an invisible boundary where particles from the Sun encounter the planet's magnetic environment. The discovery reveals important differences in how Jupiter and Earth respond to these incoming particles.
Beyond Jupiter, the results could also help scientists understand some of the most powerful events in the universe, including the extreme shock waves associated with exploding stars.
How Jupiter Protects Itself From the Solar Wind
The Sun continuously releases a stream of electrically charged particles called the solar wind. These particles travel through space at tremendous speeds, often faster than the speed at which sound waves move through the surrounding plasma. When the solar wind approaches a planet with a magnetic field, it encounters a boundary known as the bow shock.
At Earth, this boundary plays an important protective role. It slows and heats the incoming particles, helping redirect much of the solar wind around the planet. Without this process, more harmful particles could reach Earth's atmosphere, potentially making conditions less favorable for life.
Jupiter also has a bow shock, but its enormous size, powerful magnetic field, and gaseous composition make it a particularly interesting place to study how these boundaries behave. Scientists have long wanted to understand whether Jupiter handles the solar wind differently from Earth and what those differences might reveal about other objects throughout the universe.
Scientists Discover a More Complex Defense System
Using measurements from Juno, researchers discovered that Jupiter relies on plasma waves with multiple frequencies to slow and heat incoming solar particles. These different frequencies, known as "harmonics," create a more elaborate wave pattern than the one typically observed at Earth.
The process can be compared to music. Just as several notes played together produce a richer sound than a single note, plasma waves containing multiple frequencies can interact with incoming particles in more complex ways. This allows Jupiter's bow shock to transfer energy to more particles, heating them and reducing their speed.
Earth's bow shock, by comparison, primarily uses plasma waves concentrated around a single frequency. That simpler arrangement is generally sufficient for the conditions encountered near our planet.
"Jupiter has found its own way to deal with the solar wind, through plasma waves that are stronger and exhibit richer harmonic structures," says Jayasri Joseph, a postdoctoral researcher in the Department of Physics and Astronomy at Iowa and the study's corresponding author. "That's important because if you have multiple frequencies, you can heat more particles in the solar wind and slow them down."
Jupiter Has an Extra Line of Defense
The researchers identified another striking difference in how the two planets interact with the solar wind.
Before incoming particles reach Jupiter's main bow shock, they can encounter smaller shock structures called shocklets. These additional regions help slow the solar wind before it arrives at the primary shock boundary.
Earth's bow shock, in contrast, generally serves as the main region where the incoming solar wind is slowed and redirected. Jupiter's additional shock structures reveal a more complicated process for managing the energy carried by solar particles.
"Earth does not need to take these extra steps to handle the solar wind because the impact isn't as powerful," says Bill Kurth, a research scientist in Iowa's Department of Physics and Astronomy and a coauthor of the study.
Kurth has participated in NASA's Juno mission since the spacecraft launched in 2011.
What Jupiter Can Teach Us About Exploding Stars
Although these observations focus on Jupiter, their significance could extend far beyond our solar system.
Shock waves occur throughout the universe, particularly in environments where enormous amounts of energy are released. Some of the most extreme examples are found in supernova remnants, the expanding clouds of material left behind when certain dying stars explode.
These cosmic shock waves are vastly more powerful than those encountered near Jupiter. However, the physical processes that control how energy moves through plasma share important similarities. By examining Jupiter's bow shock in unprecedented detail, scientists can investigate mechanisms that would be much harder to measure directly around distant stars.
"Because even more powerful shocks occur around astrophysical objects such as supernova remnants, Jupiter's bow shock offers a nearby natural laboratory for exploring and for understanding how nature converts enormous amounts of flow energy into heat and energetic particles," Joseph says.
Understanding these processes could improve scientific models of how shock waves transfer energy, heat particles, and shape environments across the universe.

If you're an organ donor, you should know about these changes comingTransplant teams can talk to families about organ donation before they've decided whether to continue life-sustaining medical care for loved ones. Until now, that has been forbidden.
Are you an organ donor? Here are some rule changes you may want to know
Organ donation conversations are changing. Critics worry families may feel pressuredListen·4:064:06Toggle more options
EmbedEmbed<iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6019613/nx-s1-9980938" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
The U.S. organ transplant system is making a controversial change to a long-standing rule that was designed to protect potential donors. The revision aims to boost donations and reduce errors. But critics worry that the move may endanger patient care.
A new proposal for organ donation sparks concern
Under the change, theOrgan Procurement and Transplantation Network, which runs the transplant system, will relax a strict firewall between the doctors and nurses trying to save patients in the hospital and the transplantation team standing by to procure patients' organs.
Previously, no one from that team was even supposed to talk to family members until after they had made the heart-wrenching decision to let a loved one go. The rule was intended to prevent pressure that could change the care patients receive. It was also in place to dispel any doubts that doctors aren't doing everything they can to save patients.
But the board of directors for the transplant system voted Aug. 20 to modify that rule as part of anew set of guidelinesgoverning donation followingcirculatory death. That occurs after life-sustaining care has been withdrawn and now accounts for about half of organ donations.
The new rules, which go into effect Nov. 18, "allow discussions for organ donation to take place once end of life discussions are taking place with the potential deceased donor's agent," according to the new policy.
Why is the firewall previously barring these conversations coming down?
"I think the best way to think about it is that insisting on a bright line without focusing on what's happening on either side of that line is a false sense of security," Dr. Raymond Lynch, the director of transplantation at theHealth Resources & Services Administration, the federal agency that oversees the organ network, told NPR in an interview.
The new rules aim to prevent disturbing mistakes that have occurred in the past. Those errors have includedpatients being wheeled into operating rooms to remove their organswhen they were still alive.
'Horrifying' mistake to take organs from a living person was averted, witnesses say
"That specific line in the policy is part of a suite of improvements to the coordination and communication between the organ procurement organizations and the healthcare team that is caring for these patients in hospitals and the families of the patients themselves. And that really is a marked improvement over the policy that was in place before," Lynch says.
In addition to allowing donation teams to approach families sooner, the new policies include making it easier to pause organ retrieval if anyone becomes concerned that something is amiss and standardizing other patient protections, including testing for determining death.
"Documentation, clear coordination, deference to the primary healthcare team and consequences — that's what keeps patients safe," says Lynch.
The change in policy is also designed to make sure the organ retrieval team isn't brought in too late to conduct the tests and preparation necessary for families to honor their loved one's desire to be a donor.
When that happens, "the family loses out on that memory" of helping their loved one donate their organs, "the patient loses out on the choice that they made, and the people on the waiting list lose out on the chance to receive a lifesaving organ," Lynch says.
More than 109,000Americans are waiting for an organ transplant, according to the Health Resources & Services Administration. About 12 die every day because of a chronic organ shortage.
Does the change cross an ethical line?
Critics, however, say the change is dangerous. It could subtly pressure families and caregivers to discontinue care and create confusion about who's in the intensive care unit to try to save their loved one and who's there to obtain their organs, which could deepen distrust in the organ donation system.
"It's a very important bright line," says Dr.Lainie Ross, a bioethicist at the University of Rochester. "Our primary responsibility is that patient's well-being and care. And we need a bright line. That's where our focus is, and we're not even going to start thinking about whether those organs are usable until death is inevitable and imminent."
Doctors try a controversial technique to reduce the transplant organ shortage
She adds: "When my family member is in that hospital bed, I want to know that we're all on Team Mom and not worried the reason the doctor's really suggesting the treatments aren't working is because they want your organs for someone else."
Ross says she's "horrified to think that families will feel pressured. They'll feel manipulated."
Others also see problems with the change.
"I don't disagree with the desire to have more transplantable organs. I think transplants provide great benefit to many, many people," says Dr. Claire Morgan, a transplant surgeon who serves on the transplant network'sPatient Affairs Committee. "But people may be pressured to make that decision too quickly. I don't want to interfere with a family's grieving process, and I don't want to interfere with a family's ability to make a decision for their family member at a time when it's correct for them."
Some critics say the change is the latest worrisome development for organ donors.
"This is part of a number of things that are going on in organ donation that are blurring lines," saysLois Shepherd, a professor of law and bioethics at the University of Virginia who opposed the change as a member of the working group that developed the new guidelines. "A lot of safeguards for patients are weakening. And that's a concern to me."
But the change was endorsed by theAssociation of Organ Procurem

fact_units.text: Here’s What to Know About the Impending Impact | WIREDSkip to main content
After 22 yearsin orbit and afailed rescue missionthis summer, it is highly likely that the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory will crash into Earth sometime next week.
It is not known where on the planet the spacecraft—which is roughly as big as a large elevator—will fall.
Despite its size, experts say the risk to the public is relatively low.
What is now a useless piece of space junk was for a long timeextraordinarily valuableto the scientific community.
Launched on November 20, 2004, Swift was a space observatory equipped with three telescopes.
It was designed primarily to detect and studygamma-raybursts, which are among the mostenergetic explosionsin the universe.
Swift would locate these events and transmit their positions to observatories around the world for further study.

The observatory was designed to operate for a few years in low Earth orbit, but it far exceeded its expected lifespan, helping to make many important discoveries about theevolution of the cosmos, including the study of supernovas and thedestruction of starsby black holes.
However, in 2024, increased solar activity heated and expanded the upper layers of Earth’s atmosphere, increasing the drag on the satellite and accelerating its descent.
Without apropulsion systemcapable of correcting its orbit, its days were numbered.
In July 2026, NASA launched a special $30 million mission to rescue Swift.
A robotic spacecraft called LINK was supposed to drag Swift away from Earth by 150 miles, giving it a higher orbit and thus extending its operational life.

In August, NASA administrator Jared Isaacman explained that the difficulties that led to the mission’s cancellation were due toproblems with the spacecraft’scontrol system, which made it impossible to keep it properly oriented and stable in space.
On October 26, NASA announced that Swift was less than 170 miles from Earth’s surface—a very low orbit for a satellite.
According to the agency, thetelescopes on boardcould no longer maintain stable observations of their astronomical targets.
Swift conducted its final observation on October 20, then the operations team based at Pennsylvania State University terminated its operational status.

“Swift delivered an incredible, lasting return on investment for the nation, designed for a two-year primary mission but productive for more than 10 times as long,” Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of the Astrophysics Division at NASA headquarters in Washington, saidin a statement.

“In that time, Swift played a major role in advancing our understanding of the changing universe and was part of a revolution in astrophysics that showed how critical rapid-response observations are to the entire community.”
In its lifetime, the satellite observed over 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and nearly as manysupernovas, data from which contributed to more than 7,000 research papers.
“Swift leaves us with anextraordinary archiveof multiwavelength observations that will fuel new discoveries for decades more,” Domagal-Goldman added.
The Swift satellite is shown in July 2004 at Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral, Florida.
The US Space Force estimates Swift is likely to crash on or around Friday, November 6—or at least whatever remains of the satellite will.
Most of the space observatory is expected to disintegrate as it reentersthe atmosphere.
However, some pieces made of tungsten and parts of the mirrors could survive that chaotic process, Brad Cenko, NASA’s chief scientist for the mission,told the Associated Press.

“The most likely survivors are its six heavy reaction wheels, the spinning flywheels it used to aim itself, along with tougher telescope parts such as lenses and mirrors,” Dean Sladen, a quality manager and aerospace engineer at Accu Components,said to Space.com.
“Only a handful of small, scorched fragments are expected to make it down—nothing recognizable as a telescope.”
Large areas of Africa, Australia, India, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America fall within the reentry zone monitored by the Space Force.
If there is a more precise calculation, that information has not been made public, but it’s most likely that all Swift’s remaining pieces will end up in the ocean.

“NASA's own orbital debris requirements state that the risk of human casualty fromsurviving debrisshall not exceed one in 10,000, so it is highly likely this work has been completed but not published,” Sladen said regarding therisk assessment.
“Personally, I believe it should be published, as NASA has done with previous satellites.
The risk is almost certainly very small, but it would give people a clear, factual picture rather than guesswork.”

To dive or not to dive? Football's big dilemma after Alexander Isak non-penalty - BBC Sport
Were Arsenal lucky not to give away a penalty?
ByDale JohnsonFootball issues correspondent
Bradley Barcola delivered a cross into theArsenalpenalty area, withLiverpoolstriker Alexander Isak seemingly ready to nod home an equaliser.
The Sweden international just failed to get his head on the ball, and it drifted out of play.
Isak simply turned around to make his way back up the field in readiness for the goal-kick.
Replays showed that Jurrien Timber had a handful of Isak's shirt. Surely that prevented the striker from being able to play the ball?
Yet Isak did not complain. Without watching those replays you would have no inkling there was a potential penalty.
Referee Andy Madley did not see anything. The video assistant referee (VAR), Stuart Attwell, decided there was not enough in it for a review.
"There is a clear grab of the shirt,"Liverpoolmanager Andoni Iraola said after the1-0 defeat by the Gunnersat Anfield on Sunday.
"The answer is you have to dive, if you don't dive they won't call it."
When players do dive, they get criticised.
Take Alexis Mac Allister, described as "embarrassing" by Jamie Carragher for throwing himself to the ground, claiming he was headbutted by Noni Madueke in the second half.
You can understand Iraola's frustrations at not getting the penalty, so why did the VAR not get involved?
And do players really have to dive to get decisions?
Holding is all about the impact on an opponent
Image source,Getty ImagesImage caption,
Liverpool lost the game to Arsenal 1-0 without having a shot on target
Cast your mind back to a game betweenSunderlandandFulhamin February.
Harry Wilson swings a free-kick into the penalty area. The ball flies through toSunderlandgoalkeeper Robin Roefs, who punches it to safety.
But on the ground is Calvin Bassey, who immediately gets up and appeals to referee Craig Pawson, arms outstretched. TheFulhamplayer wants a spot-kick for a shirt pull by Brian Brobbey.
Nothing is picked up on-field but the VAR, Tony Harrington, identifies a tug on the shirt and sends the referee to the monitor to give a penalty.
There are striking similarities to Timber on Isak.
One resulted in a VAR penalty, but the other did not.
One player went to ground, but the other did not.
Rather than to dive, perhaps there is a better description of what Isak had to do: give the referee and the VAR a decision to make.
"Arsenalgot lucky," Danny Murphy said on Match of the Day. "If Isak maybe makes a bit more of it. I hate to see players exaggerate, but he's going to score. It's a big moment in the game."
Shirt pulling is not in itself an automatic foul. The determination is always about how it affects the opponent.
As the law says: "A holding offence occurs only when a player's contact with an opponent's body or equipment impedes the opponent's movement."
Indeed, the 'coat hanger effect', when a player's shirt is pulled well away from the body, is more likely to be penalised.
Still, impact is crucial. If it was not, any minor tug on a shirt would require a VAR intervention for a penalty.
And if Isak gives the impression there has been no impact, that is going to be a consideration.
Former Premier League assistant referee Darren Cann told BBC Sport: "It has to be sustained holding - some will say it was sustained, some will say it wasn't. But it's interesting that Isak didn't even appeal."
There is some annoyance in refereeing circles that the goalposts keep being moved when analysing decisions.
One moment video officials are being told that the VAR should not use slow-motion replays. And then, as was the case with Isak, slow-motion replays are used as the case for the prosecution.
There seems to be far less in the incident at full speed, that the hold of the shirt is more fleeting with minimal impact.
With the high bar for intervention this season, this may go down as an on-field error but not to the threshold for a VAR intervention.
Arsenal move clear at the top with a rare win at Liverpool
"If he goes to the floor, they call the penalty 100%," Iraola said. "It shouldn't be like this but it is what it is."
The Spaniard's comments are largely true, of course, as we saw with Bassey. But that is not always the case, especially this season.
In the summer, Uefa referees' chief Roberto Rosetti said that there were "too many reviews",which had led to attempts to play for or earn video decisions.
There is now a greater focus on players who dive or embellish contact to 'win' penalties.
The number of interventions in the Premier League has historically been the lowest in Europe, which is probably why the number of subjective reviews (14) is exactly the same as last season after nine rounds.
And with the high bar, a small amount of contact with no appeal is unlikely to lead to a review.
The flipside is why players should have to appeal? After all, this is not cricket. And we've seen plenty of surprise interventions where no player has asked for, say, a handball.
With only one missed VAR intervention, according to the Key Match Incidents Panel, in the Premier League this season, the video referees will argue they are getting the balance right.
Iraola clearly will not share that sentiment today.

‘Our Risk, Their Reward’: Zohran Mamdani on AI and Data Centers | WIREDSkip to main content
If you thinkyou had a wild year, just imagine how New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani must feel.
In October 2025, weeks before his historic election win,WIRED sat down with Mamdanifor an interview at his campaign office. I remember, vividly, the energy that he carried into the room. This was a man, after all, who’d just pulled off a stunning political feat, rising from being an unknown to becoming the mayoral front-runner in a matter of months. In part, that was because of his message, which focused squarely on affordability and the working class. But much of Mamdani’s campaign success can be attributed to how that message was delivered, namely through a mastery of social media that made every other politician in America look like they were still figuring out how to open Instagram.
Mamdani, then just about to turn 34, radiated in our first conversation with what I can best describe as a supernatural electricity. It lit up the room, and in a subsequent photo shoot on a bustling Manhattan street, drew passersby as if by magic. New Yorkers hooted and hollered at the candidate who, seemingly overnight, had made the mundanity of local politics feel like a cultural revolution.
Fast-forward one year, and the Mamdani electricity is still there—it just might be a little bit more tired. The daily grind of governing, after all, doesn’t offer quite the same excitement as a rocket-ship campaign. Not to mention that Mamdani, particularly given his massive reach online, has now become a lightning rod for polarizing conversations, from Israel to the Democratic Socialists of America, as well as a beacon of political hope for millions across the country and even around the world.
Mamdani’s approval rating among Big Apple voters sits at a stunning 69 percent, and he’s become among the most influential figures on the American left; he’s also been described, by his harshest critics, as a dangerous radical whose politics threaten the very city he’s been elected to lead. No pressure.
During a sit-down interview at New York’s City Hall, the mayor and I spoke about what he’s learned during his 10 months on the job, how he uses social media as a tool for governance, and where he stands on some of the most pressing issues facing Americans in today’s midterm elections. Mamdani might be tired—he divulged, hoarsely, that it had been “a long day”—but the internet’s Mayor also seems newly liberated, and certainly empowered to speak his mind. Winning power and wielding it, after all, are two very different things. And right now, the power is squarely in Zohran Mamdani’s corner.
Photograph: Jutharat Pinyodoonyachet
KATIE DRUMMOND: It was almost exactly this time last year that I interviewed you in your campaign office. I remember that for two reasons. One, it was just before the election, but two, you were just about to have a birthday. I was remembering that this weekend, because I was in Sunset Park on Saturday. Sunset Park, for those who don't know, is the best park in Brooklyn, and actually all of New York. I'm sure you agree.
While I was there, I saw you being serenaded with “Happy Birthday.” I did not join. I kept walking. I was like, “I’m gonna see this guy.”
ZOHRAN MAMDANI:I was wondering, like, “Who’s that woman who’s not singing along?”
Yes, the one with the really excited 9-year-old, and her mom was like, “No, we’re gonna keep going.” That was me.
Do you feel a year older? How has the last year of your life been?
It’s been a pretty incredible year. It has also been probably the most transformative year that I’ve lived in my life in terms of what my life was versus what it is now. Much of that year has been having the privilege of having the greatest job in the world. To lead this city and now to be 35.
I think 35. It’s a funny thing because in the world of my friends, this is an age that has a lot of existential questions that come with it. In the work that I do, most people are significantly older than me, and so the meaning of the age, it doesn’t really live in a professional setting.
Do you ever feel like your age is a barrier in politics?
No. When I met [Brazilian President Luiz Inácio] Lula [da Silva] during the UN General Assembly, he was very excited by the fact that I was young. [Laughs] He kept coming back, “So young!” I don’t think it’s a barrier. It’s been one that has also illuminated both the promises and the betrayals of politics.
To be 35 means you grew up through the housing crisis. You grew up through the Iraq War. You grew up through so much of what has shaped our country’s politics over the last few decades. These have been formative moments in my and so many other people’s lives. That too often politics is shaped by those for whom these are issues that just affect other people, not ones that have been all-consuming.

Data centers aredeeply unpopular. But what if we called them something else?
Axios reportsthat OpenAI is preparing a “PR blitz” for after the midterm elections on Tuesday, as Democrats seem likely to win back the House of Representatives, andpossibly the Senate, too.
The company’s chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane told Axios that the midterms will be “a bit of a movie trailer for what you’re going to see in 2028,” when he expects AI to be “theissue” in the presidential election.
So OpenAI is to influence the AI debate moving forward, with Lehane discussing several proposals, including the development ofAI “speed limits”; finding ways to help people see AI as empowering them in their daily lives; pushing the U.S. to take a role in developing global standards; and yes — rebranding data centers as “AI compute campuses.”
Lehane also described the conversation around data centers (a debate that has pushed Amazon and Microsoft to say they willno longer use NDAs in their negotiations with local governments) as “good and healthy.”
“Communities should hold companies responsible and accountable so they really and truly get a transformative benefit from these projects,” he said.

“‘29 is their official timeline,” Kirby told podcast host Monica Langley. “It’s not going to happen in ‘29—it’s going to take longer.”
Boom first made headlines for flying its XB-1 demonstrator aircraft in 2024 and 2025 to demonstrate a “boomless cruise” concept that harnesses theMach cutoffphenomenon. Such a feat involves flying just beyond supersonic speeds at higher altitudes under specific atmospheric conditions, so that the aircraft’s shockwaves refract upward and minimize the impact on the ground.
The company’s plan to revive supersonic air travel has been backed by the Trump administration via efforts to ease regulations. In June 2026, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) proposed a new ruleoverturning a long-standing banon commercial supersonic flights over the United States following anexecutive orderfrom President Donald Trump.
Boom’spressreleaseshave previously described achieving aircraft certification and carrying the first paying customers by 2029. The company has conditional agreements with American Airlines, Japan Airlines, and United Airlines involving non-refundable deposits of unknown amounts that would allow the airlines to fully purchase the Overture aircraft once it becomes commercially available.
But United CEO Kirby pointed out that Boom still has “a lot of hurdles to overcome” while developing Overture and getting the supersonic airliner certified by the FAA. “So it’s not a guarantee that they’ll overcome,” he cautioned during the podcast interview, even though he praised Scholl and the company in general.
This follows Kirby’searlier commentsback in March that put the chances of Boom’s Overture airliner entering commercial service at “50-50.” Ars has reached out to Boom for comment.
Although Boom completed building the factory intended for production of the Overture airliner in 2024, the facility, located at Piedmont Triad International Airport in Greensboro, North Carolina, has mostly sat dormant since that time. That hasraised questionsfor North Carolina state leaders who provided more than $50 million in taxpayer funding to help build the Overture factory.
Since October 2025, NASA has separately been doing test flights involving theexperimental X-59, which has a long, needle-like nose designed to reduce the sonic booms from supersonic flight. But this is a completely different approach than Boom’s use of the Mach cutoff flights.
Boom Supersonic’s prototype turbine core, called Sprint Core, is intended to power both gas turbines for AI data centers and the engine for Boom’s supersonic airliner.Credit:Boom SupersonicBoom Supersonic’s prototype turbine core, called Sprint Core, is intended to power both gas turbines for AI data centers and the engine for Boom’s supersonic airliner.Credit:Boom Supersonic
Much of Boom’s recent focus has been on developing natural gas turbines to power AI data centers as an additional revenue stream. On October 22, the companyunveiled another factoryin Centennial, Colorado, dedicated to producing a 42-megawatt natural gas turbine called Superpower for data centers.
The Trump administration’s public support of Boom was once again evident as US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright participated in the event alongside Colorado Governor Jared Polis.
Boom described its new Superpower factory as making turbine parts while still undergoing construction. It aims to deliver the first gas turbines to AI data center customers in mid-2027 while ramping up annual production to 25 turbines in 2028 and 50 turbines by 2029.
Boom’s detour into powering data centers coincides with many tech companiesprioritizing natural gasas the primary power source to get their projects up and running. Some data center developers are even using “mobile gas generators strapped to semitrucks” or “aeroderivative turbines originally designed for aircraft and warships,” according to themarket intelligence platform Cleanview.
However, Boom CEO Scholl alsoacknowledged the recent lossof a $1.25 billion deal that would have seen data center developer Crusoe purchase 29 of Boom’s gas turbines,in a poston the social media platform X on September 25. Crusoe has been involved in buildingTexas data centersforOracle,Google,andMicrosoftthat draw upon various power sources, including natural gas and renewables.
Scholl said Boom “will be delivering about 250MW of Superpowers next year to other sites” but did not specify theAI data centercustomers that may be using the gas turbines.
Still, Boom has characterized the development of a gas turbine for data centers as being synergistic with its design of the Symphony engine for the Overture airliner. During the October announcement, it also described having completed a prototype turbine core, called Sprint Core, that is intended to eventually power both the Superpower gas turbine and Symphony engine for the airliner.
That turbine core is set to undergo testing at the Colorado Air & Space Port, with Boom planning to fire the turbine for the first time before Thanksgiving. That would be a concrete development milestone, but the company still has much to do in proving it can get both its AI data center and supersonic airliner ventures off the ground.

The battle over data centers is hitting the ballot box. Brookings scholar Darrell West talks about how the backlash against the AI boom, flock cameras and tech companies is crossing party lines.
This is FRESH AIR. I'm Tonya Mosley. The AI boom has a problem. It has to be built somewhere, and to power it, tech companies are building massive data centers. They need land, enormous amounts of electricity, and in many cases, water. In exchange, they promise jobs and community investment. But people who live in these communities are demanding to know, what's this going to cost us? There's also another question, who gets to decide? In communities from Wisconsin to Louisiana, residents say local officials are negotiating data center deals without their input.
This midterm election, voters in more than 40 cities and towns across eight states will decide ballot measures on data center bans, moratoriums and requirements that residents get a vote before one is built. And Democrats and Republicans are going after their opponents for what used to be a bragging right, the ability to bring billions of dollars in investment to town. My guest is Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution. He and his colleague, Nicol Turner Lee, write about the backlash against AI data centers and how these local fights are becoming part of something much bigger, a challenge to the enormous power of the tech industry and who gets to decide what our future looks like. And, Darrell West, welcome to FRESH AIR.
DARRELL WEST: Thank you, Tonya. It's nice to be with you.
MOSLEY: Well, I actually want to start with a couple of political ads. And the first one is from Ohio, where Democrat Sherrod Brown is challenging Republican Senator Jon Husted. And Brown accuses Husted of aggressively courting data centers and backing corporate tax breaks while residents face rising electricity bills. Let's listen.

UNIDENTIFIED NARRATOR #1: Jon Husted, who's he really working for?
SHERROD BROWN: I'm Sherrod Brown and I approve this message.
MOSLEY: OK, now listen to this one. And it comes out of Wisconsin. Republican Tom Tiffany is running for governor against Democrat David Crowley. And Tiffany accuses Crowley of wanting to turn Wisconsin into a global data center hub at the expense of taxpayers and local communities. Let's listen.
(SOUNDBITE OF POLITICAL AD, "DATA CENTER DAVID")
UNIDENTIFIED NARRATOR #2: Meet Data Center David Crowley.
DAVID CROWLEY: There's an opportunity for us to really become an AI and a data hub not only for the entire country, but for the entire globe.
UNIDENTIFIED NARRATOR #2: And he wants you to pay for it. Data Center David Crowley won't roll back data center tax incentives. Our lakes run dry, family farms paved over - why? - because Crowley's campaign is funded by the people building them. Data Center David Crowley; Big Tech wins, Wisconsin pays.
MOSLEY: All right. So, Darrell, what's fascinating to me about these ads is you've got a Democrat from Ohio and a Republican in Wisconsin, and they're making practically the same attack. When did you realize this wasn't just a string of maybe local zoning fights anymore, that it really has become a national political story?
WEST: Now, Tonya, you're completely right. It has become a national political story. And public opinion has changed dramatically just over the course of the last year. As you mentioned in your intro, a year ago, politicians of both parties were falling all over themselves trying to attract these economic development dollars into their local communities. They were basically providing tax breaks to these very wealthy tech companies in order to get the data centers built there.
But over the last six to nine months, we've just seen this huge change where people either went from being mildly positive or at least neutral towards data centers, to today, 70% of Americans now say they have serious reservations about data centers. A recent survey showed 50% of Americans said they did not want to live next to a data center. And so these ads that you just showed basically demonstrate how that has changed. But it's not just Democrats versus Republicans. I mean, whoever has supported data centers in the past, whoever has supported tax breaks for data centers in the past, is now finding that policy position being used against them in this campaign.
MOSLEY: Data centers, though, they've really been around for decades. So what's different about the enormous ones that are being built now for AI?
